answer: Every change to the service follows Jimini's Secure Software Development Lifecycle. Changes move through four segregated environments (local, development, pre-production, production). A pull request must be approved by a code owner other than its author, with a successful continuous-integration run (unit, integration and end-to-end tests), and functional acceptance is carried out on staging and pre-production before promotion. Each production deployment must be approved by someone other than the change author, the approval being recorded through Git tags; emergency fixes are reviewed after the fact within 24 working hours. Production systems, container images and third-party dependencies are scanned continuously, and an external penetration test is commissioned annually from an independent third party. Internal evaluation campaigns of model answers are also run by legal experts against an internal question grid scoring legal reliability and answer quality, including hallucinations.

question: Please describe any measures used to ensure data quality and fairness across the data collection and curation stage (e.g., dataset audits, filtering training data to remove harmful content or personal information, fine-tuning on curated data, use of moderation tools, assessment of limitations to model generalisability).
answer:
Jimini AI does not train or fine-tune foundation models and does not use client data for training. Data quality work therefore concentrates on the legal corpus we curate and on the documents our users bring.
Our legal corpus is built exclusively from official and authoritative French public sources, primarily Légifrance for legislation and regulation and Judilibre for Court of Cassation case law, together with administrative and constitutional case law. Using official sources means provenance is traceable by construction and no harmful or personal content enters the corpus beyond what the public authorities themselves publish. The corpus is refreshed so that answers reflect the law in force, and every answer surfaces the underlying source so users can check it against the official text.
Client documents are processed strictly to serve the user’s own request, are logically segregated by organisation, and are never pooled, reused across clients or used to improve models. An anonymisation capability is available to users who need to remove identifying information before processing. Known limitations, including the fact that coverage focuses on French law and that outputs must be verified by a qualified professional, are documented in our code of conduct and covered in the training we deliver to users.

question: Describe key privacy measures and data-protection standards applied.
answer: Odysai SAS acts as processor for customer content (uploaded documents, prompts and outputs) and as controller for account, authentication, billing and analytics data, under a Data Processing Agreement whose Annex A lists all sub-processors. Customer data is stored in France (Scaleway, ISO/IEC 27001 and HDS; S3NS, SecNumCloud-qualified, for public administrations), backups are kept in the EU and inference is performed exclusively in the EU, with no transfer of customer data outside the EU. question: Please provide any further comments and implementation documentation.
answer:
Our platform includes an agent that plans a sequence of steps and calls tools to carry out a legal task: searching official legal sources, retrieving documents from the client’s own library, and reading or editing documents, spreadsheets and presentations. It is built on third-party foundation models that we integrate; we do not train or fine-tune models.
Autonomy is deliberately bounded. The agent runs only within a session a professional user has started, on that user’s own documents and within that user’s permissions, and it produces a draft or an analysis for that user rather than taking actions outside the platform. It cannot send communications, make payments, file documents with a court or act on third-party systems. Every answer cites the source it relies on, and the output is a draft that the qualified professional reviews and validates before use. Agent tool accuracy is measured against fixed benchmarks of realistic professional requests, scored deterministically rather than by another model, and a dedicated verification capability checks that the case law and statutory references produced by the agent correspond to existing sources.

question: How does your organization define and/or classify different types of risks related to AI?¹
answer:
Maintain an internal taxonomy, classification system, and/or set of risk area definitions
Align with specific external frameworks, standards, reports, and/or guidance documents such as taxonomies, classification systems, and/or sets of definitions for risk areas (e.g. the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the ISO/IEC 42001, the OECD AI Principles, the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, the International AI Safety Report). (please specify): Microsoft supports internationally aligned approaches to AI governance, including those that provide taxonomies, classification systems, and/or sets of definitions for risk areas. Microsoft’s Responsible AI Principles are aligned with the OECD AI Principles and are operationalized through the Microsoft Responsible AI Standard. We align with recognized standards and best practices, including the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and have achieved ISO/IEC 42001 certification for Microsoft 365 Copilot and other products, providing independent validation of our AI management system. Microsoft signed the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, a framework to support compliance with the EU AI Act’s requirements for general-purpose AI (GPAI) models, and published Microsoft's Frontier Governance Framework which demonstrates alignment with the Code’s scope of risks to be assessed for GPAI models with systemic risk. Microsoft also contributes to efforts to strengthen the shared evidence base for defining advanced AI capabilities and risks, including the International AI Safety Report.
Consult with external stakeholders (e.g., from academia, industry groups, civil society, or standard development organisations) when developing or updating risk taxonomies
Define enhanced safety measures for specific dangerous capability thresholds, that, once reached, require safeguards (e.g. capability threshold for dangerous Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear (CBRN), cybersecurity attacks, dangerous advanced autonomy capabilities, or other capabilities).

Microsoft's Frontier Governance Framework (FGF) defines specific tracked high-risk capabilities at which severe risks — unless adequately mitigated — may warrant pausing development and deployment. These are: (i) chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) weapons capabilities providing significant uplift; (ii) offensive cyberoperations capabilities providing uplift for highly disruptive or destructive cyberattacks, including on critical infrastructure; (iii) advanced autonomy, including expert-level autonomous completion of AI research and development tasks; (iv) loss of control, a model’s ability to undermine effective human control through adaptive, deceptive, or self‑reinforcing mechanisms such that, when deployed, it can no longer be reliably directed, modified, or shut down; and (v) harmful manipulation, or a model’s ability to strategically distort human behavior or beliefs at scale.
Loss of control and harmful manipulation were added as tracked capabilities in the February 2026 FGF update. Microsoft continues to advance research on evaluation methods and risk acceptance criteria for these two newest tracked capabilities. The FGF applies to AI models developed by Microsoft where the training compute exceeds 10²⁵ FLOPs. It also applies when Microsoft substantially fine-tunes a first- or third-party model and the fine-tuning compute exceeds one-third of the compute used to train the base model. Where the training compute of a third-party base model is unknown, the FGF applies a default threshold of one-third of 10²⁵ FLOPs.
For models within scope, Microsoft first monitors for leading indicators of high-risk capabilities and conducts deeper capability assessments where warranted. Each tracked capability is assessed against qualitative thresholds corresponding to low, medium, high, or critical risk levels, detailed in Appendix I of the FGF. Models assessed as low or medium risk may be deployed with appropriate safeguards. Models assessed as high or critical risk are subject to further review and additional safety and security mitigations before deployment, followed by post-mitigation assessment to ensure that residual risk has been reduced to a low or medium level. Examples of circumstances that could indicate elevated risk include:
CBRN weapons - high risk: the model provides meaningful uplift to an expert's (PhD-level) ability to develop and deliver a novel CBRN threat, or to a medium-skilled actor's ability to develop and deliver a known CBRN threat. Critical: meaningful uplift to an expert's ability to develop a highly dangerous novel threat, or significantly lowering barriers for a low-skilled actor to develop and deliver a known CBRN threat.
Offensive cyberoperations - high risk: the model meaningfully uplifts a low-to-medium-skilled actor's ability to conduct highly disruptive or destructive attacks on critical infrastructure (e.g., novel zero-day exploit chains, complex malware). Critical: it lets a low-skilled actor identify and exploit major vulnerabilities, or enables an expert, well-resourced actor to mount novel, effective operations against hardened targets.
Mitigations are proportionate to the assessed risk. If during FGF implementation Microsoft identifies a risk that cannot be sufficiently mitigated, development and deployment are paused until mitigation practices evolve to meet the risk [FGF p.8]. “High” and “critical” risk levels on any tracked capability trigger escalating security measures - from restricted access, defense-in-depth, and advanced security red teaming for “high-risk” levels, up to high-trust developer environments, hardened tamper-resistant workstations with enhanced logging, and physical bandwidth limitations between weight-containing devices and the outside world for “critical” risk levels [FGF p.7].
Risk determinations do not rely exclusively on model capability. Microsoft also considers system-level mitigations, societal and institutional factors that affect whether a hazard could materialize, and the marginal capability uplift the model provides relative to currently available tools and information, including open-weights models [FGF p.6].
The FGF sits within Microsoft’s broader AI governance program, which addresses risks across the AI models, platforms, and applications Microsoft develops and deploys. This program defines three policy categories reflecting graduated concern: Restricted uses (subject to specific AI development or deployment restrictions, defined by the Office of Responsible AI); Sensitive uses (scenarios with significant impact on life opportunities, physical safety, or human rights, requiring notification to the Office of Responsible AI and additional governance steps); and Unsupported uses (uses not designed or evaluated for, for which customer use is discouraged).
Microsoft also draws on external expertise from independent evaluators, researchers, industry groups and other stakeholders to inform and help improve its risk identification and governance approaches, including as our approach to frontier risk evolves. Following the February 2026 update to the FGF, SaferAI increased Microsoft’s safety framework score from 18% to 33%, ranking Microsoft third among frontier AI developers in its assessment of risk management industry practices. SaferAI also assessed Microsoft as best in class for overall risk identification, as well as for risk governance decision-making and transparency.
Microsoft considers the specificities of different AI technologies in designing and implementing governance. Previously, generative AI and autonomous agentic AI requirements were formalized as standalone policies, and both have been integrated into Microsoft’s re-engineered Responsible AI Standard as “scenario-specific” (versus “core”) requirements. Scenario-specific requirements are tailored to specific technologies and risks, and specific practices are defined in response to those risks (e.g., specific threat modeling practices for agentic AI). From July 2025 to June 2026, Microsoft assessed nearly 2,500 generative AI releases, 30% of which were related to agentic AI, and reviewed over 450 Sensitive Use cases, of which over 30% were agentic related.
Frontier models are addressed as another “scenario” in our Responsible AI Standard, with scenario-specific requirements mapping to our FGF. The FGF's "Advanced autonomy" capability thresholds directly address agentic risks by assessing autonomous task completion, tool use, and the ability to correct for complex error conditions [FGF p.13]. FGF capability elicitation explicitly tests models with multi-agent setups, prompt optimization, and tool/plugin connection to maximize performance on tracked high-risk capabilities [FGF p.6].

Multilingual and cross-cultural evaluation, including collaboration with local ecosystems (e.g., national AI institutes, language-specific evaluation consortia) for under-represented languages and cultural contexts (please specify): Microsoft is committed to advancing multilingual and context-relevant AI because language and cultural context are fundamental both to expanding access to AI’s benefits and to ensuring that AI systems are safe, secure, and reliable wherever they are deployed. As Microsoft highlighted at the India AI Impact Summit, language remains a significant barrier to AI diffusion, with AI systems often performing less consistently in digitally underrepresented languages than in English. Addressing this gap requires investment across the AI lifecycle - from locally relevant data and model capabilities to evaluation methods grounded in the languages, cultural norms, and real-world contexts in which AI is used. Expanding the geographic and linguistic coverage of AI research and evaluation can therefore help broaden the diffusion of beneficial AI while surfacing safety, security, and performance risks that English-first or translation-based testing may fail to capture. Microsoft is advancing these objectives through work on multilingual and multicultural evaluation, frontier safety and security, and community-centered AI research: • Microsoft is co-leading the MLCommons AILuminate benchmark’s multilingual, multicultural, and multimodal expansion in partnership with Google DeepMind, enabling more reliable measurement of AI safety and security beyond English and Western-dominant cultural contexts. The effort is currently focused on building the capability to assess performance of benchmarks in multilingual and multicultural contexts, working with partners to implement that capability in major Indic and Asian languages, with plans to develop an open source playbook that would accelerate expansion to other regions and additional APAC languages. • Microsoft contributed to the Frontier Model Forum's issue brief Emerging Practices for Multilingual Evaluations for CBRN and Advanced Cyber Risks (July 2026), which addresses the gap in safety and security evaluations for the highest-risk capabilities beyond English, and sets out best practices to build native evaluations across languages and cultures. • Microsoft is also advancing Samiksha, a community-centered method for evaluating AI behavior in real-world contexts, in collaboration with Karya and The Collective Intelligence Project in India. This work complements benchmark-based evaluation by helping incorporate the perspectives and lived experiences of the communities in which AI systems are used. • Microsoft signed a partnership with Singapore’s Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) in June 2026 to advance joint research and evaluation methodologies, including in multilingual AI safety. • Through Project Gecko, Microsoft is co-designing AI technologies with local communities in East Africa and South Asia to support agriculture, including the Paza family of automatic speech recognition models that can operate on mobile devices across six Kenyan languages, multilingual Copilots, and a Multimodal Critical Thinking (MMCT) Agent that can reason over community-generated video, voice, and text. We also launched PazaBench—the first automatic speech recognition leaderboard, with initial coverage of 39 African languages—and developed two playbooks for multilingual and multicultural capabilities, Paza and Vibhasha. This work also advances the New Delhi Frontier AI Impact Commitments, which Microsoft signed alongside other leading AI developers and Indian innovators at the India AI Impact Summit in February 2026. The commitments reinforce the importance of strengthening multilingual and context-relevant AI evaluations and collaborating with local ecosystems to develop and apply evaluations for under-represented languages and cultural contexts.

question: How does your organization monitor the interactions of AI agents under your control with other agents / assess risk from multiple agents interacting?
answer:
Governing agentic systems requires the ability to evaluate and monitor how they behave—not only before release but also after deployment in changing real-world conditions. This is especially important for agents because risks often arise from multi-step behavior: whether an agent used the right tool, followed constraints across several turns, handled retrieved content appropriately, or drifted from task boundaries over time.
Microsoft has evolved its risk management practices to account for risks increasingly shaped by access, permissions, memory, use over time, and interactions. As part of the new threat modelling techniques that Microsoft has developed for agentic AI and integrated into our Security Development Lifecycle and Responsible AI Standard [see response to above question], teams identify risks in their scenario, including risks from multiple agents interacting, such as the compromise or failure of one agent propagating through shared context, delegated tasks or interconnected tool chains.
Addressing these risks requires runtime controls as well as monitoring whether those controls are being enforced and how agents are behaving. More specifically, Microsoft has been developing and implementing measures that include assigning agents distinct identities and role-based access controls; applying runtime policies; evaluating agent performance on tasks and across end-to-end workflows; monitoring agent actions, communications and tool use, including through OpenTelemetry(OTel)-based observability traces and other metrics, event logs, and security logs; detecting anomalous behavior; and maintaining mechanisms to interrupt, restrict or disable agents when necessary.
Microsoft has also implemented capabilities across applications with agentic features, developer platforms (e.g., Foundry), and administrator tools (e.g., Microsoft Agent 365) and provided open-source tools, empowering our customers and the ecosystem to assess risks and monitor the agents and multi-agent systems they develop and deploy. For example, integrating with other Microsoft services, such as Entra and Defender, these capabilities can help developers and organizations:                                                                                                 
Manage agent identities and access: Establish distinct identities for agents and apply risk-based and role-based access controls (Microsoft Entra and Foundry Agent Identity).
Establish runtime policies, including to enable human and administrative intervention: Help customers establish and enforce controls, including to enable users and administrators to interrupt, restrict or disable an agent at runtime (capabilities available in Foundry, such configuration to require human approval before specified agent tool calls are executed, and the open-source Agent Governance Toolkit, including the Agent Control Specification (ACS), which enables policy guardrails across agent actions, tool calls, and outputs).
Protect against untrusted content and tool misuse: Limit access to untrusted resources and apply layered mitigations against risks such as indirect prompt injection (capabilities available in Foundry).
Run evaluations pre- and post-deployment: Assess task adherence, tool selection, and tool-call accuracy, end-to-end outcomes, and the effectiveness of safeguards (capabilities in Foundry and open-source tools, including ASSERT and Clarity).
Observe agent behavior and interactions, identify anomalies, and support investigation: Trace and log behaviors, events and metrics, such as agent actions, communications, tool calls; identify anomalous activity or divergence from an agent’s intended role or objective; and investigate unexpected behavior (capabilities available in Foundry and Azure Monitor).

question: Please briefly describe your organization’s decision-making process for deploying an AI model or system including: who has decision authority; what evidence and criteria are required (e.g., performance, safety/security, robustness, fairness, privacy, compliance, independent external testing, evaluation, validation and verification (TEVV) or assurance); contextual caveats or limitations required in interpreting risk evaluation metric results; what approvals/sign-offs are needed; and what safeguards (e.g., mitigations, monitoring, or phased release) must be in place to move into deployment.
answer:
Microsoft's deployment decision-making process varies by the risk profile, consistent with Microsoft’s Responsible AI Standard, which was updated in 2026 to better reflect the roles Microsoft plays in developing or deploying the models, platform services, or applications with different risk profiles.
Decision authority. For frontier models subject to the Frontier Governance Framework (FGF), as described in our response to question 1A, the decision to deploy can only be made by Executive Officers or their delegates, based on a Recommendation for Secure and Trustworthy Deployment. For technologies or use scenarios triggering Sensitive Use criteria (including consequential impacts on legal status or life opportunities, risks of significant physical or psychological injury, or risks to human rights), the Sensitive Uses and Emerging Technologies team within the Office of Responsible AI works with relevant internal teams to assess risks, develop additional mitigations where needed, and determine whether Microsoft can proceed consistent with our principles and Responsible AI Standard. For other generative AI products, Microsoft implements risk-based launch-readiness reviews that may include centralized review processes or reviews by experts within our responsible AI governance community with product teams. From July 2025 to June 2026, we conducted pre-release reviews for nearly 2,500 generative AI features or products.
Evidence and criteria. Depending on a technology’s or use scenario’s risk profile, Microsoft may require pre-deployment evaluations across performance, safety, security, robustness, fairness, and privacy. For frontier models, a leading indicator assessment using state-of-the-art benchmarks screens for early indicators of tracked high-risk capabilities; triggering indicators then lead to a deeper assessment involving capability evaluation, capability elicitation, and holistic risk assessment, resulting in a risk classification of low, medium, high, or critical against capability thresholds.
Under Microsoft’s Frontier Governance Framework, models within scope undergo independent red teaming by Microsoft’s AI Red Team (AIRT). Where specified gating criteria are met, including based on the model’s assessed capabilities, risk profile, and relevant domain-specific risks, Microsoft also engages qualified and independent third-party evaluators to conduct additional testing.
Contextual caveats. Evaluation results should be treated as decision-relevant evidence. Microsoft’s own public research recognizes that AI evaluation remains an emerging science: results can be sensitive to how constructs, tasks, contexts and metrics are defined, and performance observed in controlled benchmarks may not generalize reliably. Microsoft therefore draws on multiple, complementary sources of evidence across the lifecycle, including pre-deployment benchmarks, capability and safeguard testing, red teaming and qualitative expert assessment, complemented after deployment by ongoing monitoring, incident and user feedback, and re-evaluation as systems, capabilities or deployment contexts change, as reflected in Microsoft’s 2026 Responsible AI Transparency Report.
Approvals and safeguards. As described in our response to question 1A, frontier model deployment requires tailored state-of-the-art safety and security mitigations applied before deployment and re-assessment post-mitigation. AI technologies and use scenarios that qualify for Sensitive Use reviews or generative AI release reviews may be required to implement various safeguards depending on risk profile, including staged release, content safety guardrails and prompt injection defenses, off-by-default settings, human review in agentic workflows, in-product disclosures, and broader transparency and feedback mechanisms [e.g., Smart Impression and Copilot Voice case studies].

question: Following deployment, how do you use incident reports — including those shared by other organizations — to identify emerging issues, update risk assessments, and trigger corrective actions.
answer:
Microsoft  implements multiple channels for collecting user feedback (including through in-product mechanisms), reports of emerging issues or potential vulnerabilities or incidents, and other signals. Microsoft employees are also provided with multiple avenues to raise concerns, including an anonymous reporting channel.
Initial concerns reported or routed to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC), including via the researcher portal, are triaged and assessed by expert teams. If these concerns are assessed to warrant an investigation and potential incident response, appropriate teams are assembled and coordinated by response specialists, who manage root-cause analysis, mitigation, and communication. After an incident is mitigated, a postmortem analysis is conducted to assess and absorb the learnings from the event and convert them into long-term improvements in system robustness.
We incentivize the responsible disclosure of issues of concern, including risks and potential vulnerabilities and incidents, through our commitment to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure; bug bounty programs, which we have extended to AI products; and efforts to build community and offer public recognition through conferences like BlueHat and the Microsoft Researcher Recognition Program. Microsoft also draws on lessons shared through the Frontier Model Forum (FMF), where members exchange information on frontier-model vulnerabilities, threats and capabilities of concern; these insights can inform internal evaluations, safeguards and threat detection (more details in our response to question 3D).

These arrangements may enable approved participants to conduct defensive vulnerability analysis, controlled safety and security research, and internal defensive cybersecurity operations within defined technical and governance conditions.

Microsoft collaborates with industry peers, academia, civil society, standards bodies, governments and other public-sector institutions through a range of bilateral partnerships, multi-stakeholder initiatives and institutional forums. These engagements help Microsoft draw on external expertise, contribute to shared approaches to AI risk management, and strengthen collective capacity to identify, assess and mitigate emerging risks, including those that may have broader societal impacts. Examples include:
Frontier Model Forum (FMF). As a member of the Frontier Model Forum (FMF), Microsoft works with other frontier AI developers to advance shared approaches to managing frontier AI safety and security risks. Microsoft has contributed to FMF issue briefs and technical reports on topics including frontier AI safety evaluations, foundational security practices, risk taxonomies and thresholds, third-party assessments, advanced cyber risk, multilingual evaluation, AI agents, biosecurity, information sharing, incident reporting and incident response. In March 2025, Microsoft joined other FMF members in signing a first-of-its-kind agreement to share information about vulnerabilities, threats and capabilities of concern unique to frontier AI.
As a member of Partnership on AI (PAI), Microsoft contributes substantive feedback to PAI research and guidance and participates in multi-stakeholder convenings involving industry, civil society, academia and other experts. Over the past year, this has included engagement on emerging psychosocial risks and AI’s impact on human connection, including PAI’s report on how AI companies are handling suicide and self-harm and agentic report on real-time failure detection in AI agents and AI agent governance. This builds on earlier Microsoft contributions to PAI’s Guidance for Safe Foundation Model Deployment, which translates shared safety principles into practical and adaptable recommendations for model providers across the deployment lifecycle.
Microsoft co-founded the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) and has held a co-chair position since the organization’s founding. Over the last year, Microsoft participated in the C2PA’s ongoing efforts to advance the interoperability and real-world applicability of content provenance.
Microsoft actively participates in MLCommons work on AI risk and reliability evaluation, including benchmarks that form the AILuminate suite. Recent efforts have focused on developing tools to evaluate robustness against jailbreaks, psychosocial risk, privacy of agentic systems, and multilingual and multicultural performance. Microsoft is also contributing to the MLCommons AILuminate Global Assurance Program, which aims to translate benchmark results into assurance evidence through capabilities such as Benchmarking-as-a-Service, consistently defined objects of evaluation, and reliability labels. Together, these initiatives help progress consistent, interoperable, and applied assurance pathways that can inform governance, procurement, and compliance across AI supply chains.
Microsoft contributes to the development of international AI standards, including ISO/IEC 42001:2023 and related standards, such as ISO/IEC 42005, ISO/IEC 42006, and ISO/IEC 42007. Microsoft has achieved ISO/IEC 42001 certification across a broad set of systems, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, Microsoft Foundry, Microsoft Security Copilot, Microsoft Copilot Studio, GitHub Copilot, Dragon Copilot, and Copilot Health.
Microsoft is sponsoring the third year of the Global Perspectives on Responsible AI Fellowship, implemented in partnership with the Stimson Center, to strengthen our understanding of how AI practices can better reflect Global South priorities and help elevate fellows’ perspectives in conversations on responsible AI development. As part of the program, this year’s fellows participated in global convenings alongside policymakers and technology leaders, including a summit in Abu Dhabi, where fellows emphasized that AI systems depend on physical infrastructure unevenly available across regions; that sustainable AI adoption requires education and workforce pathways resilient to AI-driven economic change; and that public trust in AI is ultimately rooted in inclusion, access, and meaningful civic participation. This year, the program also shifted toward a forward-looking approach, supporting fellows as they explore alternative futures for scaled AI adoption and design practical, locally grounded pathways maximizing social and economic benefit while minimizing risk.
In 2025, Microsoft Research launched the Agentic AI Research & Innovation (AARI) program, building on the strong foundation of the Accelerating Foundation Model Research (AFMR) initiative. AARI supports twelve research projects led jointly by academic partners and Microsoft researchers around the world. The projects explore topics such as multi-step reasoning, improving reliability and uncertainty handling, enabling autonomous and resilient supply chains, physics‑guided 4D world modelling, and cultural misalignment in AI agents.
Microsoft supports public research through the US National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) Pilot by providing access to Azure infrastructure, AI models, and technical expertise. In the program’s second year, Microsoft and NAIRR launched a Deep Partnership track supporting “grand challenge” research projects, including many with access to Microsoft Discovery, an agentic research acceleration platform. Supported projects announced in early 2026 span fields including materials science, sustainability, semiconductor design, and biomedical research.
Microsoft is a founding member of the Appia Foundation, a Joint Development Foundation project administered by the Linux Foundation, launched as a cross-sector international initiative to develop practical, scalable conformity specifications grounded in international standards. The specifications are being designed to be applicable globally and able to support procurement scenarios and multiple regulatory regimes; adaptable across sectors, organizational sizes and AI use cases; clear about roles and responsibilities across the AI value chain; and suitable for conformity assessment with practical evaluation criteria and audit-ready evidence. Appia’s membership includes industry across sectors, and Appia's governance includes an Advisory Committee of independent leaders from academic and civil society.
Microsoft's engagements with AI Safety and Security Institutes (AISIs) from multiple regions and the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) are structured around specific evaluation and research areas. Further details are available in our responses to questions 16.A and 24.A.

question: Please provide a consolidated description of your organisation's approach to risk management across the AI system lifecycle, including how the practices identified above operate together and any cross-cutting governance, review or escalation processes. Please also indicate how often these practices are reviewed and what types of events trigger reviews and updates. Where relevant, please distinguish between different types of AI systems (e.g. generative or agentic AI).
answer:
Microsoft applies a comprehensive and layered risk management approach across the AI lifecycle, grounded in the Responsible AI Standard and supported by scenario-specific requirements for particular technologies, capabilities, and use cases. This approach is designed to uphold Microsoft’s AI principles consistently across the development lifecycle by defining policies, assigning roles and responsibilities, enabling proactive risk management, and establishing processes that reinforce responsible AI by design.
How the practices operate together.  Microsoft draws on the Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage functions of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Consistent with this approach, teams identify reasonably foreseeable risks and benefits; use red teaming, evaluations, and other measurement methods to assess risks and the effectiveness of mitigations; implement layered technical and operational safeguards; and document the evidence supporting deployment decisions. Measurement and mitigation are iterative: evaluation results inform mitigations, and systems are reassessed following mitigation to determine whether residual risks have been appropriately addressed.
The Responsible AI Standard serves as Microsoft’s internal playbook for building AI systems in alignment with its AI principles. Core requirements apply across Microsoft’s AI technologies, while additional requirements and review processes are applied according to the technology’s capabilities, intended uses, and risk profile. These include requirements for generative AI systems and models; the Frontier Governance Framework for advanced model capabilities that could pose national security or at-scale public safety risks; and the Sensitive Uses and Emerging Technologies program for higher-impact uses and novel technologies or risks.
Pre-deployment review connects these practices and supports consistent release decisions. Product teams document how applicable requirements have been met, including the risks identified, evaluations undertaken, mitigations applied, and any residual risks. Relevant experts review higher-risk or higher-impact uses and generative AI releases, and teams may be required to conduct further evaluation or implement additional safeguards before release. Depending on the risk profile, safeguards may include post-training interventions, system prompts, input and output classifiers, human review, transparency documentation, user feedback mechanisms, and phased or staged release. Post-deployment monitoring, incident reporting, user feedback, and real-world deployment experience then provide signals that can prompt reassessment and feed into improvements to products, engineering practices, and policy.
Governance and escalation. Product teams manage risk for the technologies they build. The Office of Responsible AI maintains the Responsible AI Standard and leads the development of new policies and guidance, informed by regulatory developments, pre-deployment reviews, red teaming, product roadmaps, research, ongoing monitoring, and incident response. The Responsible AI engineering function develops supporting tools and technical guidance so that policy requirements can be integrated into engineering workflows. Deployment of a frontier model rests with Executive Officers or their delegates, as described in our response to question 2.A. After release, escalation follows the severity assigned under the AI Security and Safety Bug Bar (see 23.A). Oversight structures, including the Responsible AI Council and reporting to the Board, are described in our response to question 21.A.
Review and updates. Microsoft reviews and updates its responsible AI policies, practices, tools, and individual risk assessments on an ongoing and event-driven basis. Relevant triggers include new or materially changed system capabilities; major product or deployment changes; evaluation, red-teaming, or monitoring results; reported vulnerabilities or incidents; evidence from real-world use and user feedback; advances in risk measurement or mitigation; research and horizon-scanning findings; and changes in applicable laws, standards, or regulatory expectations.
The Frontier Governance Framework includes additional review points for models within its scope. Leading-indicator assessments are conducted during pre-training, after pre-training, after post-training, and before deployment, and at least every six months thereafter for models within scope. A further capability assessment is conducted where leading indicators warrant deeper inspection, with subsequent assessments triggered by material changes to a deployed model’s risk profile. Microsoft also commits to an explicit discussion at least every twelve months on how the FGF should be improved, with material revisions published within 30 days of adoption.
Generative and agentic AI. Microsoft formalized specific internal requirements for generative AI systems in 2023 and has continued to update them as capabilities, risks, and regulatory requirements evolve. Generative AI releases are subject to pre-deployment review, red teaming, evaluation, mitigation, and documentation requirements tailored to their capabilities and deployment context. Agentic AI requires additional attention because systems may connect multiple models, tools, data sources, permissions, and memory, and may take actions with increasing autonomy over time. Microsoft therefore addresses agentic risks through system-level threat modelling, evaluation of autonomy, planning and tool use, controls governing access and permissions, and safeguards designed around the system’s deployment context. Where agentic capabilities may indicate advanced autonomy or other tracked high-risk capabilities, the Frontier Governance Framework provides for leading-indicator assessment, deeper capability assessment, proportionate mitigation, and risk-informed deployment decisions.

question: Please describe any measures used to ensure data quality and fairness across the data collection and curation stage (e.g., dataset audits, filtering training data to remove harmful content or personal information, fine-tuning on curated data, use of moderation tools, assessment of limitations to model generalisability).
answer:
Microsoft addresses data quality and fairness through layered practices spanning data selection and curation, safety post-training, evaluation, red teaming, documentation, and monitoring. The specific measures applied depend on the model, modality, intended use, and risks identified.
Dataset assessment and limitations. Teams assess relevant characteristics and limitations of the data used to develop and evaluate an AI technology. Depending on the model or system and its intended use, this can include assessing the suitability and inclusiveness of datasets, whether intended uses are adequately represented in training and test data, and whether applicable data collection and processing requirements have been met. Identified limitations inform evaluation priorities, mitigation measures, deployment decisions, and documentation for downstream users.
Safety post-training and content safeguards. Training-data interventions are complemented by safety post-training and product-level safeguards. For the MAI-Image models, Microsoft used safety post-training to shape model behaviour and applied safety classifiers to prompts and outputs to identify and restrict harmful content. The product team also used controls designed to reduce the generation of content that could infringe third-party intellectual property rights. In operation, meta-prompts, classifiers and output controls limit potentially harmful or infringing generation, including refusal to provide song lyrics or book extracts, and customer data is processed to analyze prompts, completions and images for content or patterns of use that may violate Microsoft's Code of Conduct. The same content safety and moderation tooling is made available to customers through Azure AI Content Safety. These safeguards were assessed through pre-release testing and continued monitoring after deployment.
Filtering of training data. Safety-focused filtering is applied to training datasets to reduce a model's exposure to harmful content. For the MAI-Image models, for example, categories including explicit violence and child sexual exploitation and abuse imagery were removed from training data, so that the models were less likely to learn detailed or realistic representations of such content. Microsoft also respects the Robots Exclusion Protocol and Bing's webmaster HTTP head and HTML metatag control.
Microsoft is also investing in broader linguistic and cultural coverage for AI evaluation, including work to expand AI reliability measurement across additional languages and cultural contexts. These efforts strengthen the evidence available to assess performance and safety for populations and contexts that may be underrepresented in existing evaluation datasets. Additional details on such initiatives are described in our responses to question 2 and 28.A

question: Please indicate, if relevant, the team or role responsible for overseeing secure testing and whether this responsibility is shared across multiple teams and/or functions.
answer:
Secure testing responsibility is shared across product engineering, responsible AI, and security, with testing protocols depending on the risk profile of the testing scenario, including the technology capability and evaluation approach. Microsoft's AI Red Team leads testing for the highest-risk systems and works with other security teams to assess testing risks and apply appropriate security measures for the profile of the testing scenario.
Internal testing responsibilities. Product and engineering teams conduct testing and evaluation as part of the development and pre-release review process. These teams are responsible for evaluating relevant risks, assessing the effectiveness of safeguards, documenting results, and addressing identified issues before release. Microsoft’s AI Red Team provides specialist adversarial testing of AI models and systems, including human-led testing intended to identify potential misuse, harmful outputs, security vulnerabilities, and weaknesses in existing safeguards. In 2025, the AI Red Team conducted more than 100 red-teaming operations, representing a 1.5-fold increase over the previous year. Testing combines human-led and automated approaches. Microsoft uses PyRIT, the Python Risk Identification Tool for generative AI, which supports structured and repeatable red teaming across AI models and systems. PyRIT supports testing across different modalities and interfaces and has also been integrated into Microsoft Foundry through an AI red-teaming agent. Findings from testing inform mitigations and can be converted into repeatable evaluations to assess whether identified weaknesses have been addressed.
Responsible AI oversight. Microsoft’s central pre-release oversight process verifies that identified risks have been appropriately evaluated and addressed before release. The Office of Responsible AI establishes applicable policy requirements and review processes, while responsible AI engineering teams develop tools and technical guidance to support implementation. Where a use meets the criteria for review under the Sensitive Uses and Emerging Technologies program, specialist reviewers provide hands-on consultation to identify relevant risks, define additional requirements, and assess whether further testing or mitigation is needed.
External testing partnerships. Microsoft supplements internal testing with external evaluators where independent or specialized expertise is needed. Over the last year Microsoft worked with ten firms holding general AI risk and red teaming expertise and with eight firms and government research institutes with deep expertise in high-severity risk areas, including biological, chemical and cyber weapons (see 24.A). External evaluators, including the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) and the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) under the agreements described at question 2, require credentials to send API requests for testing access. In 2026, Microsoft launched the External Red Team Alliance (EXTRA), which provides funding to 18 university labs across six continents and through which Microsoft is building a distributed network of researchers, practitioners and regional specialists who can contribute directly to red teaming where specialized expertise is needed.
Containment controls. Where possible, the Microsoft AI Red Team conducts testing in secure virtual machines and manages testing reports and results in an access-controlled environment that requires a customized access request for each operation. Testing environments are tailored to the purpose and risk profile of the assessment. Certain cyber evaluations require controlled access to cloud services, enterprise infrastructure, identity systems, or other external services to assess how AI systems operate in realistic environments and identify risks that would not emerge in a fully isolated setting. Where an assessment requires the system under test to retain legitimate access to external services, containment is complemented by monitoring designed to identify activity beyond the engagement’s authorized scope.

question: Describe key privacy measures and data-protection standards applied.
answer:
Microsoft applies privacy and data-protection measures across the AI lifecycle, from development and pre-release review through deployment, monitoring, and research. The measures applied are tailored to Microsoft’s role as developer or deployer, the relevant layer of the AI technology stack, the types of data involved, and the risks presented by the system.
Privacy-by-design governance. Privacy and security are among Microsoft’s core AI principles and are operationalized through the Responsible AI Standard and related privacy and security requirements. The updated Standard distinguishes Microsoft’s responsibilities as an AI developer and deployer and tailors requirements across models, platform services, and applications. Privacy risks are considered throughout the lifecycle, including during system design, risk assessment, pre-release review, deployment, and post-release monitoring.
Security controls. Training data and fine-tuned models are available exclusively to the customer, are encrypted at rest by default using AES-256 with the option of a customer-managed key, and can be deleted by the customer at any time. Model weights and related sensitive assets are encrypted at rest and in transit, with more stringent controls for highly capable models (see 11.E). Microsoft applies international information security standards including ISO/IEC 27001, to which Microsoft online services are certified through regular independent audit, and ISO/IEC 27017, 29147 and 30111. Microsoft Foundry supports geographic data-residency choices.
Customer and user controls. AI systems operating over organizational data are bound by the permissions already in place: Microsoft 365 Copilot respects sensitivity labels and Microsoft Purview policies, which can restrict its access to specific data or prevent it from summarizing sensitive files (see 7). Microsoft Purview provides further data security and compliance controls for generative AI applications. Through the Microsoft Privacy Dashboard, account holders can access, manage and delete their personal data and stored conversation history, and Copilot honors users' privacy choices made through cookie banners and in-product controls.
Privacy-enhancing research techniques. Where AI usage data informs research, deidentification protocols are applied, including automated scrubbing of personally identifiable information and machine-based "eyes-off" classification, so that no human researcher directly views the content of conversations; the analyses of Copilot usage described at 20.A were produced this way. Post-release monitoring and automated threat detection operate on privacy-reviewed observability platforms.
Transparency and informed use. Microsoft provides privacy statements, transparency documentation, model cards, application cards, and other notices to explain how relevant AI technologies use and protect data, their intended uses and limitations, and the controls available to users and customers. The applicable privacy policies and product-specific notices covering personal data, user inputs, and AI-generated outputs are listed in the response to question 17.A.
Transparency resources. Microsoft maintains publicly accessible materials including the Microsoft Privacy Statement, M365 Copilot FAQs, The New Bing: Our Approach to Responsible AI, Azure OpenAI Service data-privacy documentation, and Dynamics 365/Power Platform Copilot data security and privacy FAQs.

question: Please describe the main security measures your organization applies and indicate which are specific to particularly sensitive AI assets, where relevant.
answer:
Microsoft’s approach to AI cybersecurity builds on its established security-engineering practices and adds requirements, testing methods, and safeguards tailored to the distinctive risks of generative and agentic AI systems. These measures operate across the AI lifecycle, from threat modelling and secure development through pre-release testing, deployment, monitoring, and incident response.
Security engineering. Microsoft's foundational security policy is the Security Development Lifecycle (SDL), which is regularly updated in response to emerging risks, techniques and technologies. New AI-focused requirements have been implemented within the SDL, covering threat modeling, agent identity management, access control, memory safeguards, logging and reliable shutdown mechanisms. Secure AI development workflows govern the handling of access credentials and sensitive data through identity and access management controls and automated scanning. These practices operate within the Secure Future Initiative, Microsoft's multiyear company-wide security program launched in November 2023.
Defenses against AI-specific threats. Microsoft applies layered defenses that operate both before information reaches a model and before an agent acts. At the product level, enhanced classifiers, including Prompt Shields, scan inputs and outputs in real time for harmful content and prompt injection attempts, including indirect injection through content a model reads. Spotlighting, developed by Microsoft researchers and available in Microsoft Foundry, helps models distinguish trusted system and user instructions from potentially adversarial embedded content. For agents, Task Adherence evaluates whether an agent's planned actions remain consistent with the user's intent and the developer's design before those actions are executed, returning signals that developers can use to block execution, log the event or trigger human review. At the organizational policy and practice level, fine-grained permissions and access controls limit the impact of any injection attempt that succeeds, alongside threat modeling and other security practices. Question 7 provides further detail on threat modelling for agentic AI. Microsoft's AI Red Team and researchers have deepened expertise on novel attack vectors, including adversarial memory poisoning, techniques to detect backdoors in open-weight models, and AI recommendation poisoning, a threat class identified by Microsoft researchers in which hidden instructions embedded in links bias an AI system's future recommendations without the user's awareness. Alongside ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27017, Microsoft uses ISO/IEC 23894, NIST SP 800-218 and MITRE ATLAS as practical references for prompt injection, poisoned context, unsafe tool use and data access risks.
Agent identity and runtime control. At the product level, Microsoft Entra Agent ID, generally available since April 2026, binds each agent's actions to a distinct identity and allows organizations to manage credentials, enforce Conditional Access and least-privilege policies, maintain sign-in and audit logging, and monitor for anomalies or orphaned agents. At the organizational policy level, runtime policies can be configured to define which agents may invoke which tools, access which resources and perform which actions under specified conditions, including approval gates for sensitive or irreversible actions and administrative controls to activate, block or revoke agents. Observability and monitoring capabilities for agents are described at question 2 and 14.A.
Protection of sensitive AI assets. Model weights and other relevant elements are encrypted at rest and in transit to mitigate model theft risk. More stringent security controls are applied based on risk, including for protecting highly capable models. Robust physical, operational and network security measures protect cloud infrastructure, including AI datacenters enabling training and hosting of models; supplier security and privacy are governed by Microsoft's Supplier Security and Privacy Assurance program. Access to physical datacenter facilities is tightly controlled with outer and inner perimeters, subject to a least-privileged-access policy with time-limited access for personnel with approved business need; access requests are logged and retained, with data analyzed for anomalies.
Detection, response and threat landscape. AI systems are developed and deployed with capabilities for observability and security and event logging, supporting privacy-reviewed post-release monitoring, incident response and auditability. In 2025, the Microsoft Security Response Center received over 11,000 submissions, of which more than 600 escalated to full AI safety or security cases. The most frequent subjects were malicious use, CBRN risks and command injection. Prompt injection remained frequently reported, with notable growth on coding-assistant agents and agentic code-generation workflows and a rise in multimodal techniques using audio, images and QR-encoded inputs. Insights from these cases informed updates to guardrail tuning. Incident response processes and escalation are described at 23.A. Microsoft's Threat Intelligence community comprises more than 10,000 security researchers, analysts and threat hunters, and security standards are reviewed at least annually, with individual requirements updated between reviews. Microsoft products undergo third-party security assessments reflected in compliance offerings for ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27017, SOC 2 and other programs.
Insider risk. The Digital Security and Resilience Insider Threat Team (DSR ITT) focuses on insider threat detection and prevention, and Microsoft's SDL threat modeling assumes insider threats, informing privileged-access requirements. All red team operations assume insider access.

question: Please provide any further comments and implementation documentation.
answer:
Additional information supporting Question 9
Microsoft protects intellectual property, including copyright-protected content, through measures applied across the AI lifecycle: governing how training data is sourced and documented; evaluating and mitigating the risk that models reproduce or generate infringing content; and considering feedback from rightsholders when they report concerns.
Training data sourcing. Microsoft maintains a copyright policy and supporting guidance, covering data sourcing, content provenance, safeguards, and organizational roles and responsibilities. The policy establishes requirements for models entering the EU market, while the underlying data-sourcing controls are applied more broadly across relevant data-collection processes. Provenance controls guard against sourcing training data from websites or repositories determined to engage in large-scale piracy, and Microsoft does not circumvent technological protection measures when sourcing data.  Microsoft also respects the Robots Exclusion Protocol and Bings webmaster HTTP head and HTML metatag control.
Training data transparency. Microsoft publishes information about the data used to train relevant models through data summaries and model cards. During the reporting period, Microsoft published data summary cards for relevant general-purpose AI models placed on the EU market in accordance with Article 53(1)(d) of the EU AI Act, including for MAI-Image-2, MAI-Image-2.5, and MAI-Code-1-Flash. Microsoft also published disclosures for in-scope models, including MAI-Image-1 and Phi-4-Reasoning, ahead of the effective date of California Assembly Bill 2013, and published information for MAI-Image-1 in accordance with the Transparency Chapter of the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice (see 26.A). These disclosures provide rightsholders and other stakeholders with greater visibility into the categories and sources of content used in model development.
Evaluation and safeguards against potentially infringing outputs. Microsoft applies layered safeguards at the model and product levels to reduce the risk that its AI technologies generate content that may infringe third-party intellectual property rights. These include training-data measures, pretraining data processing, post-training interventions, system-level instructions, and input and output controls designed to identify and restrict requests or generated content that violates applicable intellectual property policies. For MAI-Image-1 and MAI-Image-2, Microsoft assessed risks related to potentially infringing outputs through pre-release evaluation and applied safeguards across the model and product lifecycle. This layered approach allows safeguards to operate at multiple points, from the composition of training data and the behavior of the model to the processing of user requests and the delivery of generated content.
Monitoring and rightsholder recourse. Microsoft continues to assess relevant safeguards after release through monitoring, user feedback, and reports of potentially problematic generated content. Consumer generative AI experiences provide mechanisms through which users and rightsholders can report concerns. These signals can inform investigation, corrective action, and improvements to model behavior, classifiers, product controls, and applicable policies.

question: Please describe how AI risk management is integrated into governance structures, including: which roles or bodies have advisory versus decision-making authority; which roles or bodies have final accountability for AI risk-related decisions; and how often policies are reviewed or updated (e.g., following major incidents, regulatory changes, or material updates to systems).
answer:
Governance framework.  Microsoft embeds AI risk management through a layered governance framework combining company-wide requirements, specialist review, executive decision-making and Board oversight. The Responsible AI Standard translates Microsoft’s Responsible AI principles into requirements for teams developing and deploying AI models, platform services and applications. The Office of Responsible AI (ORA), led by the Chief Responsible AI Officer, manages this framework, defines roles and responsibilities, establishes governance processes and provides guidance on legal and regulatory requirements. Day-to-day implementation is supported by engineering partners and the Responsible AI Governance Community embedded across product groups.
Specialist and advisory review. Specialist review complements requirements. Under the Sensitive Uses program, ORA works with product engineering and customer and partner solutions teams where foreseeable use or misuse meets Sensitive Use criteria, with reviews resulting in additional requirements where appropriate. ORA also provides early guidance on emerging capabilities and risks not yet addressed by formal policy, while Microsoft Research and external subject-matter experts provide research-informed advisory input. For qualifying generative AI products and features, ORA, a responsible AI engineering team, and experts from the Responsible AI Governance Community facilitate centralized or expert-led review processes. These review mechanisms operate at scale: between July 2025 and June 2026, Microsoft conducted nearly 2,500 generative AI product and feature reviews and more than 450 Sensitive Use reviews.
Executive oversight and decision-making. At executive level, the Responsible AI Council, co-led by Microsoft’s Vice Chair and President Brad Smith and the Chief Technology Officer and Executive Vice President of AI Kevin Scott, meets quarterly and oversees company-wide progress. It includes Corporate Vice Presidents from across the business, supported by division-level leaders responsible for operationalizing the responsible AI program. At Board level, Microsoft’s responsible AI leaders engage regularly with the Board of Directors through internal enterprise risk management reviews as well as engagement with the Environmental, Social and Public Policy Committee. Under the Frontier Governance Framework, for frontier models, the Executive Officers responsible for Microsoft’s AI governance program, or their delegates, make the final decision on whether to approve the recommendation for secure and trustworthy deployment. Along with other responsible AI policies and programs, the Frontier Governance Framework is subject to internal audit and Board oversight.
Review and adaptation. Policies and requirements are reviewed and updated on an ongoing basis in response to technological developments, regulatory changes, identified risks and incidents, lessons from after-action reviews and implementation feedback. The Responsible AI Standard has been progressively updated as AI capabilities, risks and regulatory expectations have evolved. Most recently, it was re-engineered to include dedicated Developer and Deployer Chapters and to distinguish core requirements from scenario-specific requirements. As part of this work, Microsoft analysed more than 100 enacted and proposed laws and refreshed its process for continuous regulatory analysis and adaptation. The Frontier Governance Framework also requires an explicit review at least every twelve months. Changes to practices are reviewed by the Chief Responsible AI Officer before adoption, and material revisions are published within 30 days of adoption.

question: If yes, describe how incident records are kept and used for follow-up (e.g., incident logs, root-cause analysis reports, internal tracking systems). You may indicate whether and how you define escalation thresholds for when incidents must be surfaced to senior leadership or external parties.
answer:
Issue records and classification. Issues reported or discovered, including through the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC), are classified against Microsoft's Vulnerability Severity and Content Classifications for AI Systems, the AI Security and Safety Bug Bar, which defines categories and severity levels for common AI security vulnerabilities and content-related issues. Each MSRC case is assigned a unique case number, and records are retained indefinitely. The Bug Bar is correlated with Microsoft's central AI risk taxonomy, so that assessment, mitigation, detection, and response use a common vocabulary before and after release.
Externally, vulnerabilities at any severity level are surfaced publicly as CVEs (“Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures”) whenever customer action is required to patch or update software. Since 2024, Microsoft also issues CVEs for cloud service vulnerabilities assessed as Critical severity even where no customer action is required (and marks them as such in the Security Update Guide and in the CVE record). Where identified risks or vulnerabilities affect other organizations, information is shared with them consistent with Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure principles.
Response and follow-up. In 2025, Microsoft formalized incident response playbooks across 13 topics, supporting MSRC, product, and legal teams in following a unified process when AI incidents arise; the playbooks are reinforced through tabletop exercises and readiness drills. At the conclusion of a response to an issue or incident, a review is typically conducted to understand the nature of the issue or incident, ensure the full scope of impact has been assessed, and track items to remediation. Reviews are presented to key executive leaders; themes are synthesized across reported issues and used to educate product teams, update engineering processes, and update policies where applicable; and findings feed back into product safeguards, including updates to guardrail tuning.

question: If yes, describe how research or good practices are shared (e.g., publications, conferences, collaborations with other sectors).
answer:
Public research and publications. Microsoft Research and subject matter experts from engineering and security teams publish their AI safety and security research, including work on evaluation-aware behavior in reasoning models, techniques for detecting backdoored models at scale, AI recommendation poisoning, and research on how generative AI use affects critical thinking in knowledge work. The Microsoft Research Sociotechnical Alignment Center has published a social-science-based measurement framework for generative AI evaluation and identified validity gaps in commonly used red teaming and LLM-as-judge metrics. Microsoft's MAI Futures team brings together multidisciplinary expertise to study the societal impacts of AI, publishing peer-reviewed research on both near- and long-term effects, drawing on real-world AI usage data.
Open-source releases and shared datasets. Microsoft contributes safety and security tooling to the open ecosystem so that others can apply and inspect it, including PyRIT for AI red teaming, RAMPART and Clarity for encoding adversarial and benign scenarios as repeatable tests, ASSERT for turning written behavior requirements into executable evaluations, TaskTracker for detecting indirect prompt injection developed with academic partners, and the Agent Control Specification for applying runtime governance across the agent lifecycle. Following the Adaptive Prompt Injection Challenge, more than 200,000 attack prompts submitted by over 800 participants were compiled into a public dataset to support continued research on prompt injection defenses.
Industry and multistakeholder fora. Through the Frontier Model Forum, Microsoft works with peers to develop and share practices for evaluating and mitigating risks related to biosecurity, cybersecurity, agentic risks and harmful AI system behavior; members have used an information-sharing agreement announced in 2025 to advance shared knowledge relevant to risk mitigation, and Microsoft co-funds the Forum's wet-lab biosafety research grants. Microsoft has also served as an industry reviewer for the 2025 and 2026 International AI Safety Reports, providing feedback to the independent scientific assessment of general-purpose AI capabilities and risks. Microsoft contributed to the Partnership on AI report Prioritizing Real-Time Failure Detection in AI Agents, published in September 2025. With MLCommons, Microsoft co-chairs the working group expanding the AILuminate benchmark across languages and cultures, supports the Jailbreak benchmark and the Psychosocial Task Force, and contributes to the development of the AILuminate Global Assurance Program. Microsoft is a founding member of the Appia Foundation, which works on AI conformity assessment across the AI supply chain and across sectors, and is a co-founder of the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity.
Government research partnerships. Microsoft has research partnerships with government research institutions in the US, UK, Australia and Singapore. In the US and UK, Microsoft has agreements with the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) to advance AI testing and evaluation, including collaborative work to test Microsoft’s frontier models, assess safeguards, and help mitigate national security and large-scale public safety risks. Our collaboration with the Australian Department of Industry, Science and Resources, coordinating through the Australian AI Safety Institute, focuses on research on human–AI interaction risks, including overreliance, emotional dependency, and user behavior in AI companion chatbots and conversational AI systems, especially for young people and vulnerable groups.
With Singapore‘s Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), working closely with the Singapore AI Safety Institute, we collaborate on the co-development of a policy framework on trusted access to frontier capabilities for cybersecurity operations and safety and security testing, as well as multilingual safety evaluation across ASEAN languages. Through these bilateral partnerships, Microsoft seeks to support more robust and reproducible evaluation methods, greater technical exchange, and stronger shared approaches to assessing emerging frontier risks.
Public transparency reporting. Microsoft publishes an annual Responsible AI Transparency Report, now in its third edition, describing how Microsoft governs AI, what it has learned and where challenges remain. The 2026 edition includes case studies tracing how individual models, platform services, and applications were assessed before release, an account of how Microsoft governs its own use of AI as a deployer, and a breakdown by impact category of AI safety and security cases reported to the Microsoft Security Response Center. Microsoft first published its Frontier Governance Framework in February 2025 and updated it in February 2026, adding disclosures on its red teaming and risk modelling practices and providing greater transparency into how Microsoft evaluates and monitors frontier model risks and engages third-party evaluators. Microsoft also publishes data summaries, model cards, and application and platform cards for in-scope technologies.

question: Provide any additional details or context on how or when users are informed they are interacting with advanced AI systems (e.g. if such mechanisms are planned, in testing, or applied only to certain products).
answer:
Microsoft employs several complementary mechanisms to ensure that end-users understand when they are interacting with an advanced AI system. These mechanisms are tailored to different products and scenarios.
User disclosures within the product interface. For applicable products, Microsoft's Responsible AI Standard requires product teams to disclose the role of AI in user interactions and to inform users that they are engaging with an AI system. In practice, these disclosures can include on-screen notices, contextual warnings, and consent flows embedded in the user experience. AI-generated responses may also include citations to source material so that users can verify information.
For example, across Copilot experiences, in-product disclosures inform users that they are interacting with an AI application. These disclosures may include notices or disclaimers about the potential for AI to make errors or produce unexpected content.
In certain risk scenarios, additional disclosures may apply. Microsoft's Sensitive Interactions Policy, which addresses open-ended conversation, memory, and personalization across sessions, requires disclaimers and factual responses, including encouragement to consult qualified professionals, when interactions relate to significant decisions such as health or finance. For AI systems acting on a user's behalf, Microsoft also surfaces actions directly in the user experience.
For example, in Copilot Cowork, actions are visible in the conversation, actions that send or modify content require explicit user approval before execution unless the user has already provided permission in their initial instructions, and outgoing messages include an attribution indicating AI assistance, so that recipients are informed when interacting with AI-produced content. Similarly, Browse with Copilot is an opt-in experience with an educational flow, preview labeling, and in-product warnings that highlight AI involvement; users can see actions in real time and interrupt or take control.
Distinct labeling of AI-generated content.  The Responsible AI Standard requires that AI-generated or AI-modified content be clearly and conspicuously disclosed where appropriate. Microsoft is scaling engineering capabilities to mark AI-generated content and attach provenance metadata across relevant product surfaces. Provenance metadata is implemented to meet C2PA's requirements for cryptographically hardened marking.
