question: Describe how provenance mechanisms are implemented and which standards or tools are used, and any collaborations or investments to improve content authentication (e.g., C2PA credentials, joint R&D projects, open-source initiatives, standard-setting groups). You may also indicate whether these mechanisms are tested for robustness against removal, tampering, or circumvention.
answer:
Implementation. Microsoft co-founded the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity in 2021 and has held leadership roles since its founding. AI-generated images from consumer tools such as Microsoft Designer include C2PA Content Credentials, and LinkedIn displays a Content Credentials indicator on signed images. Microsoft's layered strategy pairs cryptographically sealed C2PA provenance metadata with watermarking as complementary mechanisms; invisible watermarks are identifiable by specialized tools, resilient to common modifications such as resizing or cropping, and can help recover provenance information where a C2PA manifest has been removed. Over the past year, Microsoft scaled its readiness to apply both mechanisms across relevant product surfaces, with central solutions to support latency stabilization, production hardening, and monitoring at scale. Content Credentials have also proved useful in enforcement: in a Microsoft Digital Crimes Unit investigation into misuse of AI image-generation systems, provenance metadata helped investigators establish the origin of many of the AI-generated images discovered.
Standards and collaboration. Over the past year, C2PA released Content Credentials 2.3 and committed to supporting adoption across additional languages; with C2PA partners, Microsoft is working to extend provenance standards beyond an English-ready baseline. Microsoft signed the Tech Accord to Combat Deceptive Use of AI in 2024 Elections and piloted Content Integrity Tools, including a capture app developed with TruePic, enabling campaigns, election authorities, and media organizations to attach Content Credentials to authentic content.
Regulatory alignment. These mechanisms underpin Microsoft's compliance with emerging transparency requirements, including California's AI Transparency Act and other U.S. state laws as well as Article 50(2) of the EU AI Act and the EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content. The Code identifies digitally signed metadata and imperceptible watermarking as its central measures for providers, consistent with Microsoft’s layered approach. 
Robustness testing. Provenance information is only useful if it cannot easily be stripped off a file or falsified. As co-founder and co-chair of C2PA, Microsoft helps develop the Content Credentials specification. Under the specification, provenance information is digitally signed together with the file, so that any later alteration to the file or to the information attached to it breaks the signature and can be detected.
For content that carries no credential, Microsoft's AI for Good Lab, with Northwestern University and the human rights organization WITNESS, published a free test set of more than 50,000 real, AI-generated, and manipulated images, videos, and audio clips, including examples journalists and human rights defenders have encountered and examples built to fool detectors. It allows anyone to measure how a deepfake detector performs on realistic material rather than on easy test cases.
Microsoft Research's February 2026 report, Media Integrity and Authentication: Status, Directions, and Futures, tested signed metadata, watermarks, and fingerprinting across the full life of a file, from capture and editing to sharing and verification, and against attempts to defeat them, including attacks designed to make authentic content look fake. It concluded that only signed metadata can reliably show whether a file is unchanged and who signed it, and that watermarks are best used as a backup for recovering that information when the metadata has been stripped, a known limit of any metadata-based approach: provenance data can be removed through re-encoding, screenshotting, or platform processing. Building on those findings, Microsoft tests in practice whether watermarks survive common edits such as resizing and cropping, whether provenance metadata can still be verified after a file has been shared, how often detectors are wrong in either direction and how they hold up against attacks, and how people understand the signals they see. In one study, an attacker's success rate against a Microsoft AI detector fell from 41 percent to 2 percent once the detector had been trained on adversarial examples.

It sets out a forward-looking framework focused on enabling useful and capable models while preserving meaningful human control, establishing clear lines of authorization and accountability, and defining firm safety boundaries for frontier risks. The consultation invites external scrutiny of how these commitments can be made sufficiently precise, operationalized, and evaluated, including in multi-agent settings. Microsoft AI will publish a summary of the feedback received and resulting changes alongside a revised Code, with further consultations planned as the framework evolves.
Robustness, reliability, and system performance. Microsoft has invested in the science of evaluation. question: Please provide a consolidated description of your organisation's approach to risk management across the AI system lifecycle, including how the practices identified above operate together and any cross-cutting governance, review or escalation processes. Please also indicate how often these practices are reviewed and what types of events trigger reviews and updates. Where relevant, please distinguish between different types of AI systems (e.g. generative or agentic AI).
answer:
We apply a range of measures across the AI lifecycle
Plan and design - Measures include risk identification and an assessment of needs for the development process, with a focus on enterprise-relevant capabilities.
Collect and process data - Measures include Data de-duplication, filtering, and quality controls.
Build, integrate and interpret model - Measures include decentralized training with self-refinement algorithms and model merging techniques; reward models for evaluation; and parameter merging methods.
Verify and validate  - Measures include Extensive benchmarking across enterprise tasks and public evaluations; red teaming. 
Deploy - Measures include privacy and security-preserving deployment optionsincluding private and on-premises options.
Operate and monitor - Measures include, as applicable to the deployment context, isolated customer environments, vulnerability management, and security information and event management systems.
Through these measures and across the AI lifecycle, we manage risk according to three principles: evidenced risks, contextual assessment, and holistic management by design. These apply across five interconnected components: Risk Identification, Risk Assessment and Mitigation, Risk Assurance, Transparency, and Research Engagement.
Additionally, governance & Review operates across:
Escalation: Final authority over model deployments lies with Executive Leaders for model safety decisions
Reviews: Annual framework assessments or triggered by incidents/capability changes
Documentation: Maintained with version control and changelogs
For more information see our Secure AI Frontier Model Framework, available at: https://trustcenter.cohere.com/resources-details and our Command A technical report, available at https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.00698

question: Please briefly describe your organization’s decision-making process for deploying an AI model or system including: who has decision authority; what evidence and criteria are required (e.g., performance, safety/security, robustness, fairness, privacy, compliance, independent external testing, evaluation, validation and verification (TEVV) or assurance); contextual caveats or limitations required in interpreting risk evaluation metric results; what approvals/sign-offs are needed; and what safeguards (e.g., mitigations, monitoring, or phased release) must be in place to move into deployment.
answer:
OpenAI employs rigorous red-teaming processes to evaluate the performance of models and systems before external deployment. OpenAI uses both human and automated red-teaming processes. Adversarial testing involves experts who attempt to exploit the model in ways that could cause harm or lead to undesirable outcomes, or who probe the model for unexpected or unwanted behavior in a variety of domains. This process is complemented by collaborations with external organizations, such as cybersecurity firms, to provide additional perspectives and expertise in identifying potential threats.
OpenAI’s red teaming efforts include a variety of expert testing organizations that help inform our risk assessment and mitigation efforts. These organizations span a variety of domains, with diverse perspectives.
Our model review process is also informed by third-party assessments. Since our previous submission, we have published more detail on three forms of external testing: independent capability and safeguard evaluations, reviews of evaluation methodology, and direct probing by subject-matter experts. These assessments supplement our internal work and inform deployment decisions.
We use regression testing to make sure models are robust against previously discovered jailbreaks, and perform new rounds of automated red-teaming with our latest internal red-teaming attackers to validate our improvements.
Red teaming and adversarial testing are used to uncover failure modes, misuse potential, or unexpected behaviors. These findings often lead to downstream mitigation efforts — such as refining instructions, retraining, or introducing product-level safeguards.
The results of these testing activities are documented and reviewed by relevant stakeholders (e.g., model developers, product teams, risk reviewers), and actions are prioritized based on impact, feasibility, and alignment with risk thresholds.
The Safety Advisory Group reviews Capabilities Reports and Safeguards Reports, assesses residual risk and makes recommendations to OpenAI leadership, which makes deployment decisions. Findings can lead to further evaluation, stronger safeguards, access restrictions or a phased release.
We use a combination of quantitative (e.g., internal benchmarks, as well as third-party testers’ evaluations) and qualitative (e.g., subject-matter expert judgment, preparedness review outcomes, stakeholder feedback) metrics to assess AI-related risk. These are embedded in our risk evaluations. We describe some of these metrics, methodologies, and limitations in system cards and in research we publish.
It is worthwhile to note that some risks (e.g., reputational or ethical harm) resist easy quantification, and we lean on expert judgment. AI system behavior can change over time (e.g., through fine-tuning or model evolution), so risks may need ongoing validation. Additionally, risk evaluations are context-sensitive — what is lower-risk in one setting may be higher-risk in another. Risk evaluations are continually re-evaluated based on changes to the threat landscape, and in response to adverse, anomalous, or malicious activity observed on our platform.
For agentic systems, evaluation results also depend on the tools, software environment, scoring method and resources available during testing. We check for issues such as prior exposure to test material, invalid tasks and shortcuts in scoring, and interpret results within the conditions tested.

question: Please provide a consolidated description of your organisation's approach to risk management across the AI system lifecycle, including how the practices identified above operate together and any cross-cutting governance, review or escalation processes. Please also indicate how often these practices are reviewed and what types of events trigger reviews and updates. Where relevant, please distinguish between different types of AI systems (e.g. generative or agentic AI).
answer:
Plan and design: We identify how a system is intended to be used and what could go wrong, then use that assessment to decide which tests and safeguards are needed.
Collect and process data: We select, prepare and filter training data, applying relevant privacy protections and controls over where data comes from.
Build, integrate and interpret model: We test the model as it is developed and use the findings to improve its behavior and relevant protections.
Verify and validate: We examine what the system can do and safeguards’ effectiveness, using internal automated and human testing and relevant input from outside experts.
Deploy: We review the evidence and the risks that remain after safeguards are applied before deciding whether and how to release the system, which may include phased deployment to understand potential risk among a smaller audience before broadening access.
Operate and monitor: We monitor for misuse and incidents after release and use what we learn to improve safeguards and future assessments.
Evaluations are performed at multiple points throughout the AI lifecycle to ensure models are safe, effective, and align with OpenAI's objectives. In the pre-development phase, we begin with an initial risk assessment to identify potential hazards and define safety objectives, establishing a foundation for informed and responsible development. During the development phase, models undergo iterative testing to refine safety and performance as the model evolves. Before deployment, in the pre-deployment phase, we conduct a range of safety and capability evaluations, as described in our Preparedness Framework. In the deployment phase, we implement system safeguards to prevent harm and monitoring to detect unexpected behaviors or misuse, and we perform post-deployment evaluations using real-world feedback and performance data to identify emerging risks. Finally, in the post-deployment and maintenance phase, we update our evaluations and safeguards based on new misuse patterns, identified incidents, and advances in research.
We embed security controls into infrastructure and model development, and use adversarial testing, monitoring and incident review to improve them. Our work on long-horizon models has also shown why individual action checks alone can be insufficient: a sequence of seemingly acceptable actions can cross a user’s intended boundary.
Significant releases, material evaluation findings, incidents, emerging abuse patterns and changes in applicable requirements can trigger reviews and updates. Findings may change evaluations, model behavior, safeguards, access conditions or monitoring. The Safety Advisory Group advises OpenAI leadership on preparedness decisions, and relevant research, safety, security, product, legal and policy teams contribute according to their responsibilities. An explanation of the safety work for a model is published in a system card when the model is released to general availability.
Findings from internal use, evaluations and incident investigations inform our alignment work, security controls and decisions about whether work can proceed. Our September 25, 2026 report provides a further example of how incident findings change safeguards and research decisions. An internal research model accessed an external chatbot through insufficient DNS filtering in its training sandbox. Monitoring detected the behavior, but the investigation also identified gaps in detection and operational response. We stopped the affected training run and added blocking controls at two independent layers. At time of publication, training, evaluation and tool-using inference for our most capable models were paused pending validation that the gap was resolved and additional red teaming. We also committed to beginning a fresh training run with additional alignment improvements rather than resuming training of the affected model.

question: Please describe any measures used to ensure data quality and fairness across the data collection and curation stage (e.g., dataset audits, filtering training data to remove harmful content or personal information, fine-tuning on curated data, use of moderation tools, assessment of limitations to model generalisability).
answer:
Prior to deployment, OpenAI assesses and mitigates potential risks that may stem from generative models, such as information harms, or other content that violates our safety policies. We use a combination of methods, spanning all stages of development across pre-training, post-training, product development, and policy. For example, during post-training, we align the model to human preferences; we red team the resulting models and add product-level mitigations such as monitoring and enforcement; and we provide moderation tools and transparency reports to our users.
We find that the majority of effective testing and mitigations are done after the pre-training stage because filtering pre-trained data alone cannot address nuanced and context-specific harms. At the same time, certain pre-training filtering mitigations can provide an additional layer of defense that, along with other safety mitigations, help exclude unwanted and harmful information from our datasets:
We use our Moderation API and safety classifiers to filter out data that could contribute to harmful content or information hazards, including CSAM, hateful content, and violence.
For image generation systems, we filter our image generation datasets for explicit content such as graphic sexual material and CSAM.
We use advanced data filtering processes to reduce personal information from training data.
Models may perform differently across languages, tasks and groups. Evaluations, adversarial testing and feedback from use help us assess those limitations and guide further safeguards.

question: Describe key privacy measures and data-protection standards applied.
answer:
We want our AI models to learn about the world—not private individuals. We implement a series of reinforcing privacy protections to train our models from the ground up to protect private and sensitive information.
We apply filters and remove information from our training data that we do not want our models to learn from, including sites that primarily aggregate personal information. We then further train our models to reject requests for private or sensitive information, even where that information is available on the public web. We conduct a series of evaluations on our models to help ensure they align with these standards, implement robust usage policies to protect privacy, and monitor and respond to attempts to generate information in violation of these policies. We are also increasingly relying on our AI models to enhance privacy, such as to improve the filtering of personal information and augment the use of synthetic data, and are excited about the possibilities presented by this research. Our Privacy Filter is an AI tool that we use internally (and later released to the broader community as an open-weight model) to reduce the processing of personal data in the model training process, including for our most capable frontier models.
We additionally give users of ChatGPT robust and easy-to-use personal data controls, including to review and delete their data, turn off features like ChatGPT memory, and to easily opt out of content being used to further improve our models. Users can also export a copy of their ChatGPT data, giving them greater visibility into and control over the information associated with their account. We also encrypt user data at rest and in transit.
We also offer a Temporary Chat mode. Unsaved Temporary Chats do not appear in conversation history and are not used to improve our models; we may keep a copy for up to 30 days for safety purposes. Users can choose to save a Temporary Chat, in which case it becomes a regular chat and follows their account-level settings. And when using ChatGPT data to improve our models, we take a number of privacy-protective steps to reduce the processing of any incidental personal information. Our dedicated consumer privacy page provides clear, accessible explanations of these controls and directs individuals to our Privacy Portal, where they can submit requests to exercise their privacy rights under applicable law.
Beyond account-level controls, individuals—including those who do not use ChatGPT—can request the correction or removal of personal information about them appearing in ChatGPT responses. We assess these requests in accordance with applicable law and the technical capabilities of our models.
For our business services, including ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Edu and the API, we do not use customer inputs or outputs to train our models by default. We provide administrative and access controls, alongside data-retention options, with availability varying by service. Customer content is encrypted at rest and in transit. These safeguards are supported by independent assessments and certified management systems, including SOC 2 Type 2 examinations and ISO/IEC 27001 and 27701 certifications for the information-security and privacy-management systems supporting the API, ChatGPT Enterprise and ChatGPT Edu. Our Trust Portal provides supporting documentation and details of the applicable audit and certification scope.

question: Please describe the main security measures your organization applies and indicate which are specific to particularly sensitive AI assets, where relevant.

OpenAI maintains a comprehensive cybersecurity, physical security, and insider threat program governed by an enterprise risk management process and overseen by the Safety and Security Committee (SSC) of the OpenAI Foundation. Our approach integrates industry best practices with AI-specific innovations to manage the unique threats facing frontier AI systems. OpenAI aligns its information security and privacy program with ISO 27001, 27017, 27018 and 27701, supported by SOC 2 Type 2 and NIST guidance.
We have published six key measures for securing advanced AI infrastructure that complement traditional cybersecurity practices:
Trusted computing for AI accelerators
Network and tenant isolation guarantees
Innovation in operational and physical security for datacenters
AI-specific audit and compliance programs
AI for cyber defense
Resilience, redundancy, and research
We continuously assess cybersecurity risks across our systems and infrastructure. Our security controls are tailored to the risks of increasingly capable AI systems, and we adapt as we move closer to AGI. Security safeguards are reviewed regularly and refined through adversarial testing, red teaming, and ongoing research. Security controls and safeguards are also informed by changes in the threat landscape.
OpenAI treats unreleased model weights as core intellectual property. We enforce strict access controls, granting access only to individuals whose roles require it. These protections are supported by a robust insider threat detection program and secure research environments. Model weights and sensitive assets are handled exclusively within appropriately secured infrastructure designed to prevent unauthorized access or leakage. Technical controls in these environments include advanced physical security (for datacenters), cryptographic protections, real-time security monitoring, defense-in-depth network architecture, and supply chain security controls.
Security controls are reviewed continuously and iteratively—through ongoing red teaming, penetration testing, operational monitoring, third-party audits, and program-level reassessments. OpenAI engages in an independent third party audit on at least an annual basis which reviews our security measures, including our vulnerability management process.
OpenAI has a dedicated insider threat team. The program emphasizes prevention, detection, and response. This includes strong policy enforcement, employee education, access controls, monitoring mechanisms to detect anomalous or high-risk activity, and investigative capabilities.
For covered frontier models, our Frontier Governance Framework describes protections for unreleased weights including encryption, restricted access, monitoring and logging. Authorized access to model parameters is reviewed regularly. Model execution is sandboxed with safeguards tailored to the relevant workload and operating environment. Security assessments include internal and external testing.

Question 12 — vulnerability management

Question 13 — post-deployment practices
OpenAI disallows the use of our models and tools for certain activities and content, as outlined in our terms and usage policies. These policies are designed to prohibit the use of our models and tools in ways that cause individual or societal harm. We periodically update these policies in response to new risks and new information on how our models are being used. Access to and use of our models are also subject to OpenAI’s Terms of Use and our Business Terms. We employ a combination of guardrails, tools, policies, and processes to detect and enforce against abuse of our models. In addition to usage policies, we employ automated systems (for example, our Moderation API) and AI-powered tools to detect and prevent harmful content, human reviewers and expert investigators to conduct detailed investigations of model behavior and platform abuse, and external input to help our teams iterate on and regularly improve our moderation, detection, disruption, and enforcement capabilities. We publish information related to our post-deployment monitoring, mitigation and enforcement activities.
We build robust monitoring systems to detect potential model misalignment. We view model alignment as the primary lever to prevent potential misaligned behavior from our models. However, monitoring provides broad visibility into frontier model behavior, illuminating opportunities to further improve alignment and safety. This serves as an additional layer of protection against misaligned behavior that is detected.
Addressing vulnerabilities, incidents, emerging risks and misuse often requires participation from a number of teams across the company, including where applicable, teams responsible for research; safety and alignment; product; user or customer relationships and support; intelligence, investigations and teams supporting scaled detection and enforcement; security; policy teams; global affairs; legal and privacy; and communications.
Post-deployment, we rely on monitoring, user feedback, periodic security evaluations, and incident reporting to track risk emergence over time. Material findings can be fed back into model update cycles, safety classifiers, or policy adjustments.
Questions 14 and 14A — agentic systems and controls
Yes. Some of our products can perform supported tasks using tools and a cloud browser, including reading websites and completing multi-step workflows. It pauses when it needs user input, sign-in, or confirmation. Cloud browser documentation.
We design controls to help users remain in charge of an agent’s work. In our agentic products, users can manage website permissions, review consequential actions, and take over the cloud browser. OpenAI tests for prompt injection, phishing, and unintended actions, among other things.
We also train and test the agent to resist prompt injection: attempts to make it follow malicious instructions hidden in material it encounters, such as a webpage. Monitoring helps us detect and respond to these attacks. Secure browser takeover allows users to enter credentials without exposing those inputs to the model. Together, these measures address risks that arise when an agent uses outside information or works through services where the user is signed in.
Additionally, we train the model to be aligned with human intentions, and monitor for misalignment issues. This monitoring helps us detect and respond to issues as they arise in internal and external deployment, allowing us to iterate on further safeguard and evaluation development.

Graduation of mitigations: conversational scope is the primary control. question: Please provide a consolidated description of your organisation's approach to risk management across the AI system lifecycle, including how the practices identified above operate together and any cross-cutting governance, review or escalation processes. Please also indicate how often these practices are reviewed and what types of events trigger reviews and updates. Where relevant, please distinguish between different types of AI systems (e.g. generative or agentic AI).
answer:
Risk management is built into the services as layered automatic controls rather than sitting only in documents : 
- Preventive: allowlists of models, actions and tools; input validation; personal-data masking; token caps. 
- Detective: typed traces, metrics, loop detection, an alignment quality signal. 
- Corrective: fallback providers, circuit breaker, retry without tools, fail-closed bleeping, and a safe default response that hands an explicit error state back to the orchestrator rather than improvising.
The three system types are managed differently. 
- Generative: risk comes mainly from third-party model behaviour, managed by output schema validation, content-filter handling and provider fallback. 
- Agentic: bounded steps, action allowlist, loop detection. 
- The discriminative personal-data model: threshold calibration on a gold set and fail-closed design.
Above that, the six-gate lifecycle governs progression, each gate with a named condition and a named approver, and escalation running from the AI Lead to the CISO to top management.
Cadence : Every release re-runs tests and metrics. Every new model version triggers gold-set re-evaluation. Every provider change updates the allowlist. Incidents and findings trigger a fix plus a regression test. 
- Quarterly: model performance, data quality, audit findings, objectives, risk treatment, impact assessment coverage, and an operational status report. 
- Monthly: incident analysis. 
- Twice a year: supplier compliance, performance reporting to leadership, data quality review. 
- Annually: internal audit across seven areas, refreshed impact assessments, gap assessment, training completion, management review, and review of every policy. Registers and provenance records are kept at least three years or for the operational life of the system.

Bias and representativeness results must be reviewed before any production deployment, and live systems get a further data quality review at least every six months. For the retrieval-based chatbot we also track knowledge-base freshness, accuracy and completeness, and limit irrelevant context using a similarity threshold and metadata filters.

Known limitations, recorded rather than hidden.

question: Describe key privacy measures and data-protection standards applied.
answer:
Minimisation and pseudonymisation are the centre of the design, not an add-on.
The anonymisation service removes personal data from call transcripts and returns bleep ranges for the audio. Before any prompt, conversation history or tool output reaches a language model, the gateway can replace emails, phone numbers, bank details, social security numbers and URLs with reversible placeholders, restoring them only in the response that goes back to the customer. Sensitive variables can be hidden from the model entirely. Detection is deliberately tuned for recall: a word is masked as soon as it reaches a 10% probability of being personal data, and if transcript-to-audio alignment quality falls below 80% the service bleeps the whole utterance rather than risk a partial leak.
Neither shared service persists conversation content. Processing is in-memory, agent memory is cleared after each request, and the cache holds counters and identifiers only, with expiry.
Data is encrypted with AES-256 at rest and TLS in transit, with least-privilege access, per-tenant segregation and secrets held in a dedicated vault scoped per workspace. Personal data in development and test environments must be anonymised or pseudonymised unless the DPO formally approves otherwise. A data protection impact assessment is required before deploying any system that processes personal data.
Providers are treated as sub-processors with documented records confirming that no Zaion or client data trains their models. Client data remains the client's property, and its reuse for training or for other clients is contractually excluded. Customers configure masking and processing choices per workspace and per request.
Where the data sits. Production workloads run on cloud infrastructure in EU regions, with object storage encrypted server-side and reachable only through scoped roles. Managed databases run on private cloud in France - Paris, Marseille and Lyon - encrypted at rest and reachable only through private endpoints. Some legacy infrastructure remains elsewhere in the EU and is being consolidated. Cloud suppliers must hold ISO 27001 and SOC 2, confirm EU data residency, and have a data processing agreement in place.

answer:
Rakuten applies safeguards during data collection and curation to support data quality, fairness, privacy, and lawful use. Depending on the model and dataset, these measures may include reviewing data sources and usage rights, filtering or curating training data to reduce personal data and harmful content, minimizing sensitive or regulated data, and assessing data quality, representativeness, and potential bias. Feedback Loops: The Trust Layer includes mechanisms for users to report toxic or incorrect AI outputs, which are then used to refine the models.

question: How does your organization define and/or classify different types of risks related to AI?¹
answer: Maintain an internal taxonomy, classification system, and/or set of risk area definitions

Karavela develops AI models using functional MRI data to study brain function and support research into neurological and psychiatric conditions. In this context, the most relevant severe risks concern participant and patient safety, the confidentiality of brain and health data, mental privacy, and inappropriate reliance on model outputs.
 
Karavela applies the risk methodology of its ISO/IEC 27001 information security management system. Each risk is scored as probability × impact on a scale of 1 to 16. Scores of 1–4 are acceptable, scores of 5–11 are acceptable only with a treatment plan, and scores of 12–16 are unacceptable and require immediate action. AI-specific risk scenarios are included in our risk register and assessed on the same scale. This methodology is complemented by human-subject research ethics, data-protection requirements, and scientific and clinical validation. We assess the potential severity, likelihood, scale and reversibility of harm; the vulnerability of affected individuals; the intended use and foreseeable misuse; and the effectiveness of available safeguards.
 
We would consider a use unreasonable where a credible pathway to severe harm remains insufficiently controlled. Examples include:
Using an insufficiently validated model to make consequential diagnostic or treatment decisions.
Inferring or disclosing sensitive cognitive or health information outside the authorised research purpose
Enabling coercive or discriminatory uses of brain-derived information, including employment or insurance decisions.
Presenting probabilistic neural decoding outputs as reliable evidence of an individual’s thoughts, intentions or beliefs.
 
Safeguards should increase with demonstrated capabilities, access to sensitive data, deployment scale and decision-making authority. Uses with potential clinical consequences require stronger validation across participants, sessions and acquisition settings as well as assessment of failure modes and subgroup performance. Where residual risk cannot be adequately mitigated, the relevant use should be restricted.
 
For generative neural decoding, a particular concern is that plausible generated content may not faithfully reflect the recorded brain activity. Fluency must therefore not be treated as evidence of decoding accuracy. Evaluation and communication should distinguish measured predictive performance from interpretation.

question: Please briefly describe your organization’s decision-making process for deploying an AI model or system including: who has decision authority; what evidence and criteria are required (e.g., performance, safety/security, robustness, fairness, privacy, compliance, independent external testing, evaluation, validation and verification (TEVV) or assurance); contextual caveats or limitations required in interpreting risk evaluation metric results; what approvals/sign-offs are needed; and what safeguards (e.g., mitigations, monitoring, or phased release) must be in place to move into deployment.
answer:
The AI Deployment committee has decision authority when it comes to deploying AI models. 
The committee oversees the lifecycle of in-house AI developments and external AI tools being built into Malt's products across two key pillars: (1) new model/feature:  system risk classification, risks associated to the system, data protection and fundamental rights impact assessments, technical documentation check, transparency requirements check, and third-party vendor documentation (if applicable); (2) model/feature monitoring: review risks associated to the system, review incidents (if any), performance reviews and log retention audits (minimum 6-month retention). 
Before submission to the AI Deployment committee, the machine learning/product owner must compile a standardized AI System dossier containing the evaluation framework which includes notably a list of criteria, a description of what is evaluated and the assessment method, the design specification, data protection and fundamental right impact assessments, and a information security report from Malt’s information security team. 
The committee holds binding authority on system deployment under three possible outcomes: (1) approved: sign-off for deployment under specified operational parameters; (2) conditional approval: requires specific remedies (e.g., additional human-in-the-loop controls, refined dataset balancing) prior to go-live; (3) rejected / suspended: immediate block on deployment or mandate to halt an active model due to unmitigated high risk or serious incident reporting.
Safeguards include a mandatory progressive deployment scaling from 5% to 25%, 50%, and 100% user traffic, with reviews at each increment; real-time drift and error monitoring triggers an automated switch to a deterministic, rule-based fallback system.

question: Please provide a consolidated description of your organisation's approach to risk management across the AI system lifecycle, including how the practices identified above operate together and any cross-cutting governance, review or escalation processes. Please also indicate how often these practices are reviewed and what types of events trigger reviews and updates. Where relevant, please distinguish between different types of AI systems (e.g. generative or agentic AI).
answer:
Malt distinguishes between recommendation systems, generative AI and agentic AI. Generative systems receive additional controls for prompt and output security, factuality, privacy, provider processing and human review. Agentic systems, where applicable, require additional safeguards such as least-privilege access, approved tool lists, action limits, human confirmation for consequential actions and an effective interruption or shutdown mechanism. 
The lifecycle process is reviewed and updated under three circumstances: (1) when a new system version or model iteration is released, including consultation with the AI Deployment Committee for new algorithmic model baselines; (2) at least annually, including extensive independent penetration testing and a broader review of the effectiveness of governance, security, privacy, fairness and monitoring controls; (3) on an ad hoc basis, following an active model defect, vulnerability, operational exploit, material incident, significant performance or fairness degradation, major data or architecture change, new third-party dependency, regulatory development or material research finding.
For the plan and design stage, before developing or deploying an AI system, Malt defines in the design specifications its intended purpose, users, affected stakeholders, expected benefits, foreseeable misuse and potential risks. Systems are assessed in the risk mapping across privacy, security, fairness, transparency, accuracy, human rights, operational resilience and environmental considerations by the AI deployment committee. The review determines whether the system can proceed, requires additional safeguards or should not be deployed. 
In the collect and process data stage, Malt uses professional and marketplace information relevant to the service, such as skills and experience for matching and search. Malt evaluates data quality, completeness, and representativeness. Data is limited, cleaned, and tested, including for potential bias, before use. Users can correct, update, or request deletion of their information. Third-party models and AI services are subject to AI, privacy, security and contractual review. Data shared with external providers is governed by controls such as confidentiality, zero-retention policy, limited access. 
In the build, integrate, and interpret model stage, Malt’s matching systems use layered architectures combining lexical and semantic retrieval, ranking and business rules. Models, prompts, datasets, configurations and third-party dependencies are documented and versioned where relevant. Development and testing are separated from production environments, and access is controlled according to role and need. User-facing explanations focus on the purpose and limitations of AI-assisted search and recommendations rather than presenting the system as an autonomous decision-maker. Proposed candidates, and AI-generated briefs remain subject to human validation. Users can edit, reject or replace AI-generated recommendations and can use keyword search in the directory and type in manually their brief. 
Through the verify and validate stage, Malt verifies AI systems before and after material changes through a combination of automated testing, offline/online evaluation, human review, comparative experiments, security testing and fairness analysis. Malt also evaluates user group performance and potential disparities by including group analysis and counterfactual testing in which relevant characteristics are changed while professional skills and experience are held constant. These evaluations help identify differences in ranking position, visibility and exposure. 
Before release, at the deploy stage, Malt considers the evaluation results. Where appropriate, changes are introduced progressively and monitored against an approved baseline. Production systems maintain logging and traceability sufficient to investigate outputs, model versions, relevant inputs and human interventions, while respecting data-minimization requirements. Malt maintains human oversight for AI-assisted matching and recommendations. Fallback and rollback procedures are designed to allow Malt to isolate a faulty component, revert to a previously validated version or use a deterministic alternative when an AI component or external service is unavailable or behaving unexpectedly.
While in operation, Malt monitors AI systems across data quality, performance, fairness, security, reliability, user feedback and operational impact. Monitoring may include error rates, latency, anomalous behavior, user complaints, and external-provider failures. AI-related incidents may result in additional testing, changes to data or prompts, enhanced human review, rollback, temporary suspension, retraining or retirement of the affected system. Feedback from clients, freelancers, employees, researchers and other stakeholders contributes to continuous improvement.

question: Please describe any measures used to ensure data quality and fairness across the data collection and curation stage (e.g., dataset audits, filtering training data to remove harmful content or personal information, fine-tuning on curated data, use of moderation tools, assessment of limitations to model generalisability).
answer:
Malt’s proprietary matching models are  developed using first-party data generated on the Malt platform and focusing on professional information relevant to the intended purpose, such as skill and expertise. The data is collected in the context of providing and improving Malt’s services. Malt does not rely on public-web scraping for the training of its proprietary matching models.
Malt applies data-quality and data-governance measures throughout collection, transformation and curation. These include documented data source, controlled access, schema and consistency checks, moderation of inappropriate content, validation of professional attributes, monitoring of data freshness. Data pipelines and transformations are subject to quality checks and lineage controls so that material changes can be identified and investigated. In addition, non-AI business rules govern specific operational parameters, including candidate location, availability, and language skills. Where lawful and necessary, protected and aggregated sensitive personal data may be used separately for fairness testing and impact assessment. Data minimization, retention controls and access restrictions are applied to derived datasets, evaluation data and other model-related artefacts. 
To reduce the risk that historical booking patterns reproduce existing biases, Malt evaluates the quality and fairness of training and evaluation data through group analysis, counterfactual testing and audits. This includes testing whether profiles with comparable skills and experience receive different ranking positions when protected characteristics are varied. Data-quality, fairness and representativeness findings are incorporated into model development, deployment reviews and post-deployment monitoring. Material deterioration, evidence of disparate impact, data-quality failures, harmful outputs or changes in the underlying data can trigger additional investigation, corrective action, retraining, rollback or a renewed review by the relevant governance and deployment functions.

Malt integrates AI cybersecurity into its wider information-security framework rather than treating it as a separate control environment. System access is governed by role-based access control, least privilege principles, and mandatory multi-factor authentication across all corporate systems, developer repositories, and production environments. All platform data is encrypted in transit using strong cryptographic protocols (TLS 1.3) and at rest using industry-standard encryption (AES-256) across databases and file stores. Malt undergoes extensive, independent third-party penetration testing on an annual cycle to proactively identify and remediate code vulnerabilities and configuration flaws. And Malt continuously monitors its information system, including through a bug-bounty program. 
Malt classifies models, databases, prompt templates, and inputs as high-sensitivity assets requiring specialized technical controls such as filters to remove unneeded personal identifiers and confidential information; further, the information system runs on dedicated, private cloud server capacity with restricted network access controls; client project briefs, and user prompts processed via third-party generative LLMs (e.g., Gemini family) are subject to strict zero data retention policies.

question: How does your organization define and/or classify different types of risks related to AI?¹
answer:

Consult with external stakeholders (e.g., from academia, industry groups, civil society, or standard development organisations) when developing or updating risk taxonomies

We categorize the risks associated with the use of AI into two perspectives: “AI Safety,” which ensures that AI operates safely and appropriately within the scope intended by humans and prevents harm to life, physical well-being, property, mental well-being, and the environment; and “AI Security,” which protects AI from unauthorized access, tampering, damage, and data leaks from external sources. Furthermore, based on the “NEC Group AI and Human Rights Principles,” we have established a framework for assessing human rights and privacy risks from the perspectives of fairness, privacy, transparency, accountability, and appropriate use.
We identify risks arising from AI that require attention and have established and implemented company-wide policies that define governance structures and compliance requirements, as well as guidelines, manuals, and checklists that outline operational workflows. At every phase of the lifecycle—from planning and proposal through design and development to operation and maintenance—the relevant departments collaborate to implement a risk mitigation process that involves taking measures commensurate with the severity of each risk.
In our enterprise-wide risk management, we refer to the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (COSO) Enterprise Risk Management Integrated Framework and ISO 31000, and we utilize the “Risk Total Picture” framework, which classifies risks into three categories based on their nature. We update our risk map quarterly based on a five-level impact assessment and a three-level urgency assessment, and report it to the Risk Control and Compliance Committee, which is overseen by the Board of Directors. Within this framework, we have identified “Respect for Human Rights” as one of our risks. After continuously assessing both actual and potential negative impacts across the entire value chain, we have designated “New Technologies, such as AI, and Human Rights” as a significant human rights issue.
In accordance with Japan’s AI Act (Act on Promotion of Research and Development, and Utilization of AI-related Technology), and taking into account global regulatory trends, guidelines, and social acceptance, we continuously review our risk assessments, internal policies, and the implementation of countermeasures. Furthermore, we regularly convene an advisory council comprising external experts to seek ongoing advice on AI and human rights risks posed by new technologies and forms of application, such as generative AI, biometric authentication, and AI agents. We incorporate these insights into our deliberations on risk management strategies for new forms of application.

question: Please briefly describe your organization’s decision-making process for deploying an AI model or system including: who has decision authority; what evidence and criteria are required (e.g., performance, safety/security, robustness, fairness, privacy, compliance, independent external testing, evaluation, validation and verification (TEVV) or assurance); contextual caveats or limitations required in interpreting risk evaluation metric results; what approvals/sign-offs are needed; and what safeguards (e.g., mitigations, monitoring, or phased release) must be in place to move into deployment.
answer:
Prior to deploying AI systems, we implement the following measures from a multifaceted perspective, including AI governance, quality control, and security.
1. Risk Assessment Based on AI Governance and Human Rights Policies
In accordance with the “NEC Group AI and Human Rights Principles,” we conduct risk assessments using risk checklists and implement countermeasures at every phase of the lifecycle—from planning and proposal through design and development to operation and maintenance. Additionally, based on the “AI Guidelines for Business,” we apply and update these guidelines within our internal AI governance framework.
2. Development Management and Quantitative Standards Based on the AI Quality Guidelines
To ensure the quality of AI-powered systems, we have been applying the “NEC AI Quality Guidelines,” established in December 2019, to development projects since April 2020. These guidelines establish specific standards and checklists for each of the four development phases (1. System Planning and Proof of Concept (PoC), 2. Data Collection and Processing, 3. Model Creation, Evaluation, and Testing, and 4. System Operation). By conducting checks when transitioning between phases, we proactively prevent risks in the subsequent phase. In particular, by setting quantitative standards for the volume of training data, as well as for outliers and missing values, we ensure clarity in these standards and enable objective assessments by third parties.
3. Evaluation and Safety Measures for the Generative AI Core Technology “cotomi” and AI Agents
Regarding “cotomi,” our in-house generative AI core technology, we verify the model’s safety and reliability under a comprehensive evaluation framework that utilizes multiple assessment tools—including general-purpose benchmarks, Japanese-language benchmarks, and RAG performance evaluations—while ensuring strict compliance with laws and regulations regarding training data. In addition, we have implemented high-precision AI guardrail functions, including technologies for detecting false and misleading information and proposing corrections. Furthermore, with our AI agent technology “cotomi Act,” we leverage our accumulated knowledge on risk mitigation to configure and operate agents in accordance with corporate rules and policies from a governance perspective, thereby enabling the safe and secure use of autonomous agents.
4. Security in Development and Operations
In accordance with the “Basic Information Security Rules (NEC Security Policy),” we conduct evaluations in a secure environment equipped with necessary security measures—such as isolation from external networks and authenticated access—as a prerequisite for deployment. Additionally, depending on the system’s criticality (security level), we require or recommend that our in-house security team perform vulnerability self-assessments and penetration tests. Furthermore, regarding security risks—including those associated with AI systems—we implement risk management based on a cybersecurity checklist at every phase, from the planning and proposal stages through design and implementation, to operation, maintenance, and lifecycle management. The project manager and organizational manager verify the status of these implementation efforts.

question: Following deployment, how do you use incident reports — including those shared by other organizations — to identify emerging issues, update risk assessments, and trigger corrective actions.
answer:
To maintain the safety and reliability of our AI models and systems and to mitigate risks, we operate an integrated framework that encompasses the collection and analysis of incident and threat information, vulnerability management, industry and global collaboration, post-deployment operations and customer support, and quality improvement.
1. Deployment of AI Models and Systems
We have established a CSIRT (Computer Security Incident Response Team) under the CISO (Chief Information Security Officer) to monitor cyberattacks, analyze the characteristics of attacks and malware, preserve and analyze data in the event of an incident, investigate the causes, and resolve the situation.
2. Provision of AI Models and Systems
Through the “Cyber Intelligence Sharing Platform,” we rapidly share threat intelligence—including cyberattack methods, incident cases, vulnerability risk metrics, and security countermeasure indicators—with each business division, where it is utilized as a basis for assessing business risks.
In addition, we have established the NEC Group Information Security Incident Response Desk, which receives and manages reports of security incidents. The desk includes experts in security, legal affairs, and public relations, who provide response advice from various perspectives. By operating a system that collects vulnerability information regarding products and customer deliverables and distributes patch information, we ensure a rapid response to newly identified vulnerabilities and incorporate these findings into the revision of our guidelines.
For post-deployment maintenance and operational support, we maintain and operate programs that monitor logs and implement countermeasures appropriate to the level of risk. Furthermore, we have established it as standard company practice to report and explain issues to each customer using our AI systems and to implement improvements when problems are confirmed. We participate in the “AI Safety Evaluation Environment Task Force” operated by Japan AISI, sharing insights and providing feedback within the industry based on our trial use of AI safety evaluation tools, including automated red-team functions.

question: Please provide a consolidated description of your organisation's approach to risk management across the AI system lifecycle, including how the practices identified above operate together and any cross-cutting governance, review or escalation processes. Please also indicate how often these practices are reviewed and what types of events trigger reviews and updates. Where relevant, please distinguish between different types of AI systems (e.g. generative or agentic AI).
answer:
Since there was no space to list “specific practices” in Question 7 above, we did not answer that question this time.
Throughout the entire lifecycle of AI systems, we implement comprehensive risk management by combining cross-functional governance at the executive level, multi-layered risk checks based on policies and guidelines, regular review and update processes, and management measures specific to generative AI and agentic AI.
1. Cross-functional Governance, Risk Management Throughout the Entire Lifecycle, and a Review and Evaluation Framework
The risk management framework, centered on the Risk Control and Compliance Committee and the CRCO (Chief Risk & Compliance Officer), updates the risk map quarterly based on a five-level impact assessment and a three-level urgency assessment, and provides oversight at the executive level.
We apply the “NEC AI Quality Guidelines” (which are updated regularly to accommodate generative AI) and have established specific criteria for each of the four distinct phases of development: planning and PoC, data collection and processing, model creation, evaluation, and testing, and system operation. By conducting checks when transitioning between phases, we proactively prevent risks that could arise in the next phase.
Throughout all phases of the lifecycle—planning and proposal, design and development, and operation and maintenance—we utilize risk checklists based on the “NEC Group AI and Human Rights Principles” to identify human rights and privacy risks and incorporate cross-functional measures to address them.
With regard to security risks involving AI systems, we implement risk management based on cybersecurity checklists at every phase—from planning and proposal through operation, maintenance, and lifecycle management—and identify risks, evaluate countermeasures, and conduct reviews at each phase.
2. Review Frequency and Update Triggers
Internal rules, such as the “NEC AI Quality Guidelines,” are updated regularly (e.g., to enhance the checklist for generative AI), and we have established “recognition of new threats arising from technological advancements” and “changes in the social environment” as triggers for these updates (e.g., we have updated our policies in response to the increased risk of copyright infringement in image-generation services).
In accordance with directives from the high-level information security strategy council, we periodically review our company-wide measures.
3. Management Measures Specific to Generative AI (cotomi) and Model Evaluation
For the generative AI core technology “cotomi,” we implement a multi-layered management system that combines strict compliance with laws and regulations regarding training data, a comprehensive evaluation framework utilizing multiple evaluation tools—including general-purpose and Japanese-language benchmarks as well as RAG performance metrics—and AI guardrail functions.
Based on Japan AISI’s “Guide to Evaluation Perspectives on AI Safety,” we are developing an AI guardrail that covers all of the evaluation items outlined in the guide.
We operate a system that combines vulnerability assessments using AI red teaming and penetration testing with continuous verification of outputs through anti-hallucination features.
4. Management Measures Specific to Agentic AI (e.g., cotomi Act)
Based on the insights gained so far regarding risk mitigation, configuring and operating agents in a manner that takes corporate governance rules and policies into account constitutes a unique management measure that distinguishes this approach from conventional generative AI.
In “cotomi v3”, we are working to ensure compliance with the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and improve task decomposition and tool selection capabilities. At the same time, we have developed Agentic AI for system risk assessment and internal information security audits, which supports the entire process from threat and vulnerability detection to the formulation of countermeasures.

question: Describe key privacy measures and data-protection standards applied.
answer:
We have established and published the “NEC Privacy Policy,” which complies with the Act on the Protection of Personal Information and “JIS Q 15001: Personal Information Protection Management Systems—Requirements,” and we have implemented management systems and technical measures throughout our entire group, both in Japan and overseas.
1. Basic Policy, Applicable Standards, and Company-wide Implementation Framework
We obtained Privacy Mark certification in October 2005 and have been continuously maintaining and renewing it (we completed our ninth certification renewal in October 2021).
We designate a person responsible for managing personal information in each department that handles personal information, take measures to ensure that personal information is not handled beyond the scope necessary to achieve the specified purposes of use, and strive to prevent leaks, loss, and damage through necessary and appropriate security measures.
Based on our cybersecurity checklist, we protect privacy and data throughout the entire development lifecycle of our products, systems, and services. Key measures include identifying and assessing risks to protected assets such as personal information, trade secrets, and authentication credentials; clarifying the division of responsibilities with customers and defining SLAs; implementing access control based on the principle of least privilege; encrypting stored data, backups, and communication channels; ensuring secure cryptographic key management; preventing the output of confidential information in logs and applying masking; restricting the use of confidential information in test data; monitoring access during operations; deleting unnecessary accounts and access rights; and performing irreversible data erasure when disposing of media. This checklist incorporates the principles of ISO/IEC 15408 and draws on the privacy and security management measures outlined in NIST SP 800-53.
We also require third parties with whom we share or outsource data to comply with security measures equivalent to those of our Group.
 2. Technical Safety Management Measures
We implement access control based on identification and authentication, measures to prevent unauthorized external access, and encryption during transmission (such as TLS), tailored to the risks associated with each operational phase.
We prevent information leaks in the event of theft, loss, or accidental transmission by applying storage device and file encryption (encryption at rest) as the default security level across the entire NEC Group and by appropriately configuring access rights and usage expiration dates.
To meet customers’ security requirements and data sovereignty demands, we offer multiple deployment options—including on-premises, the domestically developed and operated cloud “NEC Cloud Storage (St)” (limited to domestic data centers), and hybrid models—providing choices that help avoid the risks associated with the cross-border transfer of highly confidential data.
We provide a filtering function for sensitive information and personal information when entering prompts into generative AI systems, and have established a mechanism that allows users to proactively protect their data according to their risk level.
3. Privacy-Enhancing Technologies (PETs) and Advanced Research and Development
We are conducting research and development on “highly secure federated learning,” which combines federated learning—a technique that utilizes training data from various organizations in a distributed manner rather than aggregating it in a single location—with secure computation, which enables computational processing while the data remains encrypted. We are advancing research on this technology to prevent the inference of training data from model parameters while also avoiding a decline in AI accuracy.
At our lab, we are conducting research on a technology that combines differential privacy with federated learning to provide a theoretical guarantee that training data cannot be inferred from model outputs.
We are working on synthetic data generation technology that can be used for training and validating AI models without using real data (creating synthetic data that reproduces statistical characteristics using generative AI).
We are conducting research and development on technologies that enable training without disclosing confidential data during additional training (fine-tuning), and have successfully demonstrated the ability to run “cotomi” for inference in a confidential computing environment.

question: Please describe the main security measures your organization applies and indicate which are specific to particularly sensitive AI assets, where relevant.
answer:
Based on a company-wide cybersecurity governance framework overseen by the CISO (Chief Information Security Officer) and compliance with international standards and specifications, we implement the following security measures for AI (Security for AI) and multi-layered protection measures for high-value and highly confidential AI assets:
1. Company-wide Cybersecurity Governance Framework, Standards, and Shared Infrastructure
Based on the “NEC Group Information Security Statement,” the “Basic Information Security Rules,” and the “Cybersecurity Management Rules,” we have clarified our accountability structure to establish and maintain the ISMS (ISO/IEC 27001), and we implement security measures for customer-facing systems, products, and services. Under the oversight of the CISO, the CSIRT (comprising four teams: Threat Intelligence, Incident Response, SOC, and Development) is responsible for monitoring, analyzing, and investigating cyberattacks to determine their causes. PSIRT operates a vulnerability information management system and a permanently open reporting channel (psirt-info[at]mlsig.jp.nec.com), and publishes response information under an early warning partnership with JPCERT/CC and other organizations. We have also established a framework for collaboration between the cybersecurity department and the information security administrators in each business division.
We comply with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, ISO/IEC 27001, and the “Cybersecurity Management Guidelines Ver. 3.0.” We conduct quarterly (four times a year) vulnerability assessments, review countermeasures twice a year at information security strategy meetings, and perform regular cyber risk assessments by a Red Team.
We have implemented multi-factor authentication, passwordless authentication, EDR/NDR, DLP, and file encryption company-wide based on the Zero Trust Model (CISA Maturity Model).
2. Security Measures for AI (Security for AI)
We are systematically advancing our efforts along three pillars: “Governance (Establishing Policies and Rules),” “Management (Reviewing and visualizing compliance requirements),” and “Security Infrastructure (AI Asset Detection = Shadow AI Detection, AI Vulnerability Assessments and Audits, AI Guardrails).”
Referencing Japan AISI’s “Guide to Red Teaming Methodology on AI Safety” and the OWASP AI Testing Guide, we conduct verification of attack scenarios—such as prompt injection (direct and indirect) and jailbreak—in a controlled, isolated environment, while also performing penetration testing on systems, including large language models (LLMs). Additionally, we have set the automation of attack diagnostics by the AI Red Team as one of our key objectives.
For “NEC Generative AI Service,” used internally, we have implemented prompt input restrictions based on information confidentiality classifications, as well as a system that logs all input and output in a manner that allows for continuous auditing.
The mandatory cybersecurity checklist includes items specific to AI systems, and we are implementing the necessary measures for each project.
3. Special Protective Measures for Highly Confidential and Valuable AI Assets (Training Data, Models, Inference Environments, etc.)
Sensitive AI assets (such as data, model weights, and inference environments) are managed using secure storage (access control, encryption, and audit trail management) and are provided in on-premises or dedicated cloud environments within a dedicated data center. This ensures that access to high-value AI assets is restricted to a controlled environment, including through secure, private connections to public clouds.
We are working to ensure confidentiality at the hardware level by running “cotomi” inference on a confidential computing environment (using a Trusted Execution Environment, or TEE).

question: How does your organization define and/or classify different types of risks related to AI?¹
answer:

(please specify): Infosys aligns its AI risk classification and management approach with internationally recognized frameworks and standards, including the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), ISO/IEC 42001, OECD AI Principles, relevant EU AI regulatory requirements, and broader Responsible AI, privacy, cybersecurity, and risk management practices. Risks are categorized across areas such as fairness, safety, security, privacy, transparency, explainability, accountability, compliance, robustness, and societal impact.
Consult with external stakeholders (e.g., from academia, industry groups, civil society, or standard development organisations) when developing or updating risk taxonomies
Maintain an internal taxonomy, classification system, and/or set of risk area definitions

Our organization does not rely on a single quantitative threshold to determine when AI risks become unreasonable. Instead, severe risks are assessed through a risk-based governance framework aligned with ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), ISO/IEC 23894, OECD AI Principles, and applicable regulatory requirements, including the EU AI Act. Risks may be considered unreasonable or intolerable when they have the potential to cause significant harm to individuals, society, organizations, or critical systems and cannot be reduced to an acceptable level through technical, operational, legal, or organizational controls.
Risk assessments evaluate factors such as potential impact severity, likelihood of occurrence, scale of affected stakeholders, reversibility of harm, regulatory implications, human rights impact, safety concerns, privacy implications, cybersecurity risks, and the effectiveness of available mitigations. AI systems identified as presenting severe residual risk are subject to enhanced governance review, additional controls, deployment restrictions, or may be prohibited from deployment until risks are adequately mitigated.
Examples of potentially unreasonable or intolerable risks include:
AI systems that could cause significant safety impacts to individuals or critical infrastructure.
Systems that may result in unlawful discrimination, bias, or denial of fundamental rights.
AI applications involving unauthorized processing or exposure of sensitive personal or confidential information.
Autonomous or agentic systems capable of taking consequential actions without appropriate human oversight, accountability, or control mechanisms.
Systems that could materially facilitate cyber-attacks, fraud, misinformation, or other harmful activities.
Mitigations are applied proportionate to the level of risk and AI capability. Our organization uses a Responsible AI framework aligned with the EU AI Act, classifying use cases as Prohibited, High, Medium, or Low Risk in our AI Management System( AIMS). Prohibited (Unacceptable Risk) use cases, or those whose risks cannot be adequately mitigated, are considered unreasonable and may be redesigned, or rejected. The Responsible AI Assessment Team provides independent oversight, with high risk use cases requiring stronger controls, including enhanced risk assessments, human-in-the-loop approvals, explainability measures, security testing, privacy reviews, monitoring, escalation procedures, and executive-level governance oversight. 
The organization recognizes the distinct risk profiles of different AI technologies. Generative AI systems are assessed for risks such as hallucinations, misinformation, intellectual property concerns, privacy exposure, toxicity, and prompt injection attacks. Agentic AI systems receive additional scrutiny due to their ability to autonomously plan, make decisions, interact with external systems, or execute actions. Such systems are subject to stronger governance controls, approval gates, human oversight requirements, access restrictions, monitoring, and periodic reassessments before and after deployment.

Fujitsu regards both socio-economic and environmental risks from AI as important issues and is pursuing research, development, and investment to address each. For socio-economic risks, Fujitsu recognizes unfair AI decisions, bias, privacy infringement, misinformation and disinformation, deepfakes, and misuse of generative AI as risks that can undermine trust among individuals, companies, and society. Fujitsu therefore advances research and development in AI ethics governance, AI fairness, AI risk assessment, AI security, and misinformation and disinformation countermeasures. Fujitsu identifies compliance with laws and guidelines, Ethics-by-Design and AI governance, addressing bias in generative AI, and tackling social issues as pillars of its AI ethics technologies.
As concrete measures to reduce socio-economic risks, Fujitsu develops and provides Fujitsu AI Ethics for Fairness to verify and improve fairness in AI training data and decisions, AI ethics impact assessment to identify and evaluate ethical risks before designing AI services, and AI risk management tools. To address the societal challenge posed by the spread of misinformation and disinformation associated with generative AI and synthetic content, Fujitsu is developing a countermeasure platform that integrates misinformation and disinformation detection, evidence collection, analysis, and evaluation, aiming to contribute to a trustworthy digital society.
For environmental risks, Fujitsu recognizes that the expansion of AI technologies, including generative AI, is increasing data center power consumption and affecting the global environment. Fujitsu is therefore conducting R&D on power-saving AI computing infrastructure. Specifically, Fujitsu is researching and developing AI Computing Broker to improve GPU operating efficiency, next-generation CPU FUJITSU-MONAKA combining low power consumption and high performance, and water-cooling technologies to address increasing data center heat generation.
Fujitsu has also developed generative AI reconstruction technology to reduce the size and power consumption of large language models and strengthen its large language model Takane. This technology reduces memory consumption by up to 94% through 1-bit quantization, maintains 89% of accuracy compared with before quantization, and achieves three-times faster processing. This enables large generative AI models that previously required four high-end GPUs to run quickly on one low-end GPU, thereby contributing to power savings in AI operations. 
In this way, Fujitsu works to minimize risks while expanding the benefits of AI to society by advancing R&D in AI ethics, fairness, security, and misinformation and disinformation countermeasures for socio-economic risks, and by promoting power-saving, lightweight, and high-efficiency AI computing infrastructure for environmental risks.

question: Please provide a consolidated description of your organisation's approach to risk management across the AI system lifecycle, including how the practices identified above operate together and any cross-cutting governance, review or escalation processes.
