Criteo's AI Product Development and Deployment Guidelines govern the full lifecycle of AI in Criteo products, whether they are developed internally or by a third-party. Every new AI project undergoes a risk analysis review. Development follows secure SDLC practices; models are validated against dedicated datasets and tested in controlled environments before release. In operation, systems are monitored (including drift and train/serve-skew monitoring and security monitoring), with human oversight maintained and the ability to override, isolate, or switch off any non-compliant AI. Third-party AI tools require a legally reviewed agreement and internal authorization before use with Criteo data.  The Guidelines are reviewed and updated regularly and in case of technological and regulatory change, with approval by the Legal team.
Applicable practices in the system lifecycle stages: 
Plan and design: Standard kick-off process for each development project ensures architecture validation, vetting any third-party tool used, and risk analysis (privacy, security, ethics...)
Collect and process data: Verify that data can be used legally and contractually; apply data minimization, anonymization/de-identification/pseudonimization, encryption and appropriate access protections; filter data
Build, integrate and interpret model: Use rigorous development and validation ML methodologies and appropriate statistical techniques; regularly update models to reflect changing conditions; follow standard SDLC practices; verify licensing and confidentiality protections for training data, foundation models and model outputs.
Verify and validate: Test and validate the AI product in a controlled and monitored environment before release; test under a variety of conditions and validate the performance of the AI components; use dedicated datasets for models and agents validation and gather user feedback to identify necessary improvements to agents.
Operate and monitor: Monitor for model drift or sudden change in behavior and train/serve skew continuously where technically possible; maintain the ability to fix observed issues and override, modify, isolate or turn off the system when needed; alerting in place with on-call responsibles to fix issues; clients and users have channels to report issues which are processed according to our escalation processes.

Formal thresholds : We apply a documented risk methodology (ISO/IEC 27001 §6.1.2–6.1.3, in force in version 1.0). Criticality = likelihood × impact on a 4×4 matrix, retaining the highest impact across confidentiality, integrity and availability.  Four bands graduate both the deadline and the conditions for accepting a risk :  1 to 3 acceptable as it stands , 4 to 6 treatment within 12 months or reasoned acceptance by the direction,  8 to 9 treatment within 3 months, acceptance only with a documented compensating control , 12 to 16 immediate treatment, no acceptance in any state. That top band is our operational definition of an unreasonable risk.
Limits set at zero :  No client engagement data and no directly collected contact data pass through AI tools, only professional information already public on the open web,  no client data entered into our platform ever passes through an AI tool,  no AI tool performs an outbound action.
Answered by design :  Our compliance software embeds, calls and trains no AI model,  it is a deterministic rule engine, recorded as such in our ISMS scope. A compliance determination that is not reproducible is a risk we judged unacceptable to place in a client's hands. question: Please briefly describe your organization’s decision-making process for deploying an AI model or system including: who has decision authority; what evidence and criteria are required (e.g., performance, safety/security, robustness, fairness, privacy, compliance, independent external testing, evaluation, validation and verification (TEVV) or assurance); contextual caveats or limitations required in interpreting risk evaluation metric results; what approvals/sign-offs are needed; and what safeguards (e.g., mitigations, monitoring, or phased release) must be in place to move into deployment.
answer:
Evidence :  Before adoption, each third-party AI tool is assessed in writing against our security policy, contractual terms, model-training settings, data retention, international transfers, connectors, account security. The residual risk is stated explicitly.

Caveat on metrics : As a deployer we have no visibility into a third-party model's internals and run no model-level evaluation. Our assurance comes not from what a model scores but from bounding what it can reach and what it can do.
Safeguards : Data-minimisation rule fixing what may never be processed  per-action permission gating,  no autonomous outbound action,  validation by a named human before any output leaves. Permanent restrictions, not a release phase.
After deployment :  AI events fall under our security incident procedure and register, the AI-tool account is covered by the quarterly access review  risks are re-examined at the quarterly management review.

On the table above. Our single published channel is open to anyone, which is why most rows are marked as available ad hoc rather than as standing arrangements. question: Please provide a consolidated description of your organisation's approach to risk management across the AI system lifecycle, including how the practices identified above operate together and any cross-cutting governance, review or escalation processes. Please also indicate how often these practices are reviewed and what types of events trigger reviews and updates. Where relevant, please distinguish between different types of AI systems (e.g. generative or agentic AI).
answer:
We deploy AI, we do not build it , with no model metrics to rely on, our assurance comes from containment rather than measurement. Two boundaries,  what may enter an AI tool, and what may leave it. Every other practice serves one of them.
Our chain : A written supplier evaluation feeds a direction decision, which fixes the limits before use  data-minimisation in, per-action gating and named human validation out. In operation, anything anomalous enters an append-only incident register at detection. Each entry carries a root cause  structural causes are carried into the risk treatment plan rather than closed locally, and the affected risk rating is re-examined.
Cadence : Management and access reviews quarterly,  restoration test half-yearly, policy review and awareness session annually.
Triggers between cycles : Any recorded incident,  a new AI tool,  a supplier changing sub-processor , a structural root cause,  a regulatory change, as with the recent revision of the EU AI Act calendar.
By type : Generative use,  the severe risk is an incorrect regulatory statement reaching a client or the public, controlled by primary-source verification and human validation. Agentic use, the severe risk is autonomous action, controlled by per-action gating, no outbound action, and periodic review of the connector surface.

answer:
Not applicable at the training stage : We collect and curate no training data, run no fine-tuning, and operate no moderation tooling. Dataset audits, training-data filtering and generalisability assessment belong to the model developers whose systems we deploy, not to us.
On fairness : our compliance platform is a deterministic rule engine. It cannot acquire bias from data. Identical inputs always yield identical classifications, and every result is traceable to the rule that produced it.

question: How do you protect privacy and prevent your systems from disclosing confidential or sensitive data across the AI lifecycle?

Other(s) (specify): Our strongest privacy control is architectural rather than technical, a data-minimisation rule fixes what may never enter an AI tool. No client engagement data, no data entered by clients into our platform, and no directly collected contact data is processed through any AI system , only professional information already public on the open web. AI-assisted deliverables are produced on anonymised templates completed outside AI tools. Our compliance platform embeds, calls and trains no AI model, so client data never reaches a model by design.

question: Describe key privacy measures and data-protection standards applied.
answer:
Framework :GDPR in both of our roles,  controller for our own processing, and Article 28 processor for the data our clients enter into our platform. Security follows ISO/IEC 27001. We work from EDPB and French supervisory authority guidance.
Records and agreements. Article 30 records maintained for both roles, controller and processor. A model Article 28 data processing agreement for the processor role. Our suppliers' agreements were fully reviewed and archived.
Technical measures : Encryption in transit, TLS 1.2 minimum with HSTS. Multi-tenant isolation enforced by systematic filtering on every data query and covered by dedicated test suites. Role-based access control with server-side guards. Systematic audit logging recording identity, organisation, address and before/after detail.
Breach handling : Supervisory authority within 72 hours under Article 33, affected clients within 48 hours under our agreement, with the notification decision recorded either way.
For AI specifically: the measure is exclusion rather than protection, client data never enters an AI tool, and our platform embeds no model, so it never reaches one.
Limits, stated plainly : Encryption at rest is delegated to our infrastructure provider ,  application-level field encryption is under evaluation, not in place. Automated purge of audit logs at twelve months is decided but not yet implemented.

The AI tool provider went through the same supplier evaluation as any other, the residual risk was accepted by the direction in writing, the account used for AI tools is covered by the quarterly access review, and AI-related events fall under our general incident procedure and register. On delegation , physical and environmental security and encryption at rest are delegated contractually to our infrastructure providers, whose agreements we reviewed and archived in 2026. No such delegation exists towards the provider of the models we use : we hold no data processing agreement with it, and we say so rather than let the checkbox imply otherwise. question: Please describe the main security measures your organization applies and indicate which are specific to particularly sensitive AI assets, where relevant.
answer:
Framework. An ISO/IEC 27001 information security management system, in force in version 1.0 
Access and identity : Least privilege, need-to-know, attributability and revocation by default as stated principles. Role-based access control in the application with server-side enforcement, multi-factor authentication on supplier accounts, and a quarterly access review covering unknown users, unknown tokens and authorised third-party applications.
Application and data : Tenant isolation enforced on every data query and covered by dedicated test suites. Modern password hashing, anti-forgery protection, data access through an ORM rather than assembled queries, input validation, a full set of security response headers, and distributed rate limiting. Encryption in transit at TLS 1.2 or above.
Secrets and supply chain : No secret in source code, configuration by environment variables, secret files excluded from versioning, and a "zero secret in the repository" check at every internal audit. Dependencies pinned to exact versions with a traced vulnerability watch and defined correction deadlines.
On particularly sensitive AI assets. We hold none in the usual sense, no model weights, no training datasets, no proprietary model. What is sensitive is narrower, the credentials granting access to the third-party AI tools we use, and the source code of our deterministic rule engine. Both fall under the regime above · private repositories with multi-factor authentication, secrets never committed, and the AI-tool account included in the quarterly access review.
One limit: Encryption at rest is delegated to our infrastructure providers,  application-level field encryption is under evaluation and not in place.

We evaluate suppliers, not models. Each AI tool is assessed before use and the residual risk is accepted in writing by the direction. Clients get more : A security posture document on request, and full answers to supplier security questionnaires.
Plain language is our default, not an add-on : We write for data protection officers and compliance leads, in French and English. We publish nothing that needs machine learning expertise to read, because we produce nothing of the kind.

question: Please describe how AI risk management is integrated into governance structures, including: which roles or bodies have advisory versus decision-making authority; which roles or bodies have final accountability for AI risk-related decisions; and how often policies are reviewed or updated (e.g., following major incidents, regulatory changes, or material updates to systems).
answer:
Advisory versus decision : Our methodology draws the line explicitly , analysis may be prepared with tool assistance, decision belongs to the direction. Written supplier evaluations, risk ratings and incident findings are advisory inputs. None of them decides. We have no advisory body and no committee, and we do not describe our own judgement as one.
Final accountability :  For now,  the direction owns every risk in the register and signs every acceptance of residual risk. The memo bringing the management system into force carries a name, a place and a date. Accountability here is a signature, not an org chart.
Cadence :  Management review and access review quarterly. Backup restoration test half-yearly. Policy review and awareness session annually.
Between cycles, four things force a review. An incident whose root cause proves structural rather than one-off. Adoption of a new AI tool, which requires its own evaluation and its own decision. A supplier notifying a change of sub-processor. A regulatory change,  the revision of the EU AI Act timetable was entered as an external-context input at our management review rather than noted and forgotten.

Our management system also institutes an annual awareness session that applies to the founder and is attested like any other control. It falls due within the first annual cycle and has not yet been held (we report the state, not the intention).

Incidents are recorded in a single living register governed by a documented procedure. Entries are append-only,  a correction is made by adding, never by erasing, and an event requalified as a false alarm keeps its trace because the requalification is itself part of the evidence.
Each entry carries the detection, a severity grade, a factual description, a timeline, preserved evidence, a personal-data assessment with the notification decision, a root-cause analysis, corrective actions with owner and deadline, the lessons drawn, and a closure validated by the direction. Where a root cause proves structural rather than one-off, the corrective action is carried into the risk treatment plan rather than closed locally.
The register is internal and stays internal. In the interest of accuracy, it holds no entry to date (the process is in force).

Governed by the Responsible AI Feature Deployment and Operations Policy. 
Decision authority: the AI Governance Committee (AIGC) — a cross-functional body of senior leaders from Legal, Compliance, Privacy, Security, Product & Design, and Engineering & Data, empowered by executive leadership. The Chief Technical Officer provides the final go/no-go deployment decision.

question: Please briefly describe your organization’s decision-making process for deploying an AI model or system including: who has decision authority; what evidence and criteria are required (e.g., performance, safety/security, robustness, fairness, privacy, compliance, independent external testing, evaluation, validation and verification (TEVV) or assurance); contextual caveats or limitations required in interpreting risk evaluation metric results; what approvals/sign-offs are needed; and what safeguards (e.g., mitigations, monitoring, or phased release) must be in place to move into deployment.

Our organization uses a defined governance process before deployment of an AI model or system.
The AI Lab designs, develops, tests, and validates the solution.
Business stakeholders, Data Protection, Quality Assurance, and Security representatives review risks in their areas of responsibility.
The Digital Committee performs an independent review before deployment. The Digital Committee has authority to approve, reject, or request additional controls for significant AI use cases.
Before deployment, the project team must provide evidence for:
Functional performance.
Security controls.
Privacy controls.
System robustness and reliability.
Compliance with applicable requirements.
Risk assessment results.
Test, evaluation, validation, and verification activities.
Known limitations and residual risks.
Risk evaluation results must be interpreted in the context of the intended use, operating environment, data quality, available controls, and identified limitations. Risk metrics alone do not determine deployment approval.
The following approvals can be required before deployment:
Business Owner approval.
Data Protection approval, when applicable.
Quality Assurance approval, when applicable.
Digital Committee approval for significant AI use cases.
Before deployment, the organization must implement appropriate safeguards. These safeguards can include:
Technical and procedural risk mitigations.
Access controls and authorization limits.
Human oversight measures.
Monitoring and logging controls.
Incident management procedures.
Usage restrictions and operational guardrails.
Additional testing and validation activities.
The organization can restrict deployment scope or delay deployment if the identified controls are not sufficient to reduce risk to an acceptable level.
After deployment, the organization continues monitoring activities and reviews the solution regularly to verify compliance, performance, and effectiveness of controls.

The objective is to develop practical approaches that organizations can use to evaluate whether Human-in-the-Loop controls are effective in real-world regulated workflows.

question: Please describe the main security measures your organization applies and indicate which are specific to particularly sensitive AI assets, where relevant.
answer:
Organization-wide measures. We operate a risk-based security program with periodic risk assessments reported to senior management, and hold ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certifications alongside annual SOC 2 Type II examinations (reports via trust.anthropic.com). We maintain a threat-actor register and externally validated threat models spanning endpoint, supply-chain, physical, cloud, privilege-escalation and exfiltration vectors, and red-team AI-specific risks such as prompt injection. Baseline controls include multi-factor authentication and least-privilege, role-based access; managed-device access controls, endpoint detection and response, and application allowlisting on workstations; encryption at rest and in transit; network segmentation and data-loss controls; centralized logging with automated anomaly alerting; peer review and automated security analysis of code; continuous vulnerability scanning, risk-based remediation, annual external penetration testing, a public Responsible Disclosure Policy and bug bounties; layered physical security at our facilities and review of cloud service providers' independently audited data-center controls; and incident-response and business-continuity plans with escalation procedures for high-severity incidents, tested annually.
Measures specific to particularly sensitive AI assets. Our most sensitive AI assets are the weights of our most capable models; related training data and source code are restricted on a least-privilege, business-need basis. Weights additionally receive the ASL-3 protections our Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) commits us to maintain or improve, designed to protect against most non-state attackers: multi-party, time-limited authorization using hardware security keys; device authorization limiting weight-system access to approved managed devices; egress bandwidth controls making large-scale exfiltration more time-consuming and detectable; cloud storage restrictions designed to prevent weights being written outside our security perimeter; network-source restrictions on privileged resources; additional review and commit-integrity requirements for critical repositories; and encryption, access logging and automated detection of unauthorized weight access or movement. Third-party partners hosting these models must implement equivalent security controls.
Personnel and insider risk (organization-wide). We apply pre-employment background checks where legally permissible; confidentiality agreements binding employees and contractor personnel before access is provisioned; security-awareness training at hire and annually, supplemented by AI-incident-response training for relevant staff; and a formal insider-risk program with internal monitoring, documented investigation and escalation procedures, and confidential and anonymous reporting channels, including RSP-noncompliance reporting with protection from retaliation.
Assurance. We publish RSP Risk Reports every three to six months and a Frontier Safety Roadmap of security goals; our Frontier Compliance Framework and "Activating ASL-3 Protections" report give more detail.
We run a dedicated insider-risk program under the security standards in our Responsible Scaling Policy: role-proportionate pre-employment verification, least-privilege access to model weights and sensitive assets with logging and monitoring, mandatory security training at hire and annually, and defined escalation channels to our Insider Risk and Security teams, including anonymous RSP noncompliance reporting. Our Frontier Safety Framework (FSF) is a set of protocols that aims to address severe risks that may arise from the high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models. It complements Google’s suite of AI responsibility and safety practices, and enables Google’s AI innovation and deployment consistent with our AI Principles. 
The FSF is built primarily around frontier model capability thresholds called “Critical Capability Levels (CCLs).” These are capability levels at which, absent mitigation measures, frontier AI models may pose heightened risk of severe harm. We identify CCLs for two kinds of risks: misuse risk and risks related to machine learning R&D and misalignment. For each type of risk, we define a set of CCLs and a mitigation approach for them. Where relevant, we also define Tracked Capability Levels (TCLs). TCLs are meant to capture significant risks that may manifest at a lower capability threshold than our CCLs and we apply our mitigation and risk acceptance determination process proportionately.
Specificities of Generative and Agentic AI Systems
Because we understand that advanced and novel AI systems require evolved testing paradigms, we implement specific governance frameworks, and forward-looking policy frameworks and recommendations, to address the unique capabilities of agentic and generative AI.
Novel AI Testing: We formed a dedicated Novel AI Testing team to spearhead evaluations at scale for new AI systems—such as advanced agents and Personal Intelligence.
The TRUST Framework: To govern the capabilities of agentic AI, we introduced the TRUST framework, which is built on five core pillars: Transparency, Reliability, Unified protocols and standards, Safety and security, and Task augmentation, to guide development in this space.
Security Frameworks: We expanded our Secure AI Framework to address the rapidly emerging risks posed by autonomous AI agents. SAIF 2.0 extends our proven AI security framework with new guidance on agent security risks and controls to mitigate them. 
Regulatory Sandboxes: For high-stakes agent deployments, we recommend that policymakers leverage tools like regulatory sandboxes and pilot programs to collect real-world data on failure modes.

question: Please provide a consolidated description of your organisation's approach to risk management across the AI system lifecycle, including how the practices identified above operate together and any cross-cutting governance, review or escalation processes. Please also indicate how often these practices are reviewed and what types of events trigger reviews and updates. Where relevant, please distinguish between different types of AI systems (e.g. generative or agentic AI).
answer:
Integration Across the AI System Lifecycle
Our risk management practices operate together in a continuous feedback loop:
We take a research-driven, scientific approach to identify current and emerging risks across new modalities, codifying these inputs into a risk taxonomy.
We proactively address risks through rigorous guidelines—such as content safety policies, the Prohibited Use Policy, the Secure AI Framework, and the Frontier Safety Framework—intended to prevent harmful outputs and guide model behavior.
We stress-test systems against these frameworks using scaled evaluations alongside internal and external red-teaming.
We mitigate identified risks through supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and out-of-model mitigations like safety filters and conditional system instructions.
Post-launch, we use automated systems and human reviews to monitor for misuse.
We have mature incident management and crisis response capabilities to rapidly mitigate and remediate where needed, and feed this back into our risk identification efforts.
Cross-Cutting Governance, Review, and Escalation Processes Our governance process is grounded in a system of cross-cutting governance bodies and review forums to manage escalations and approve launches.
Our multi-layered process includes launch reviews for both frontier models and applications developed using these models.
Model releases are specifically approved by Google DeepMind’s Launch Review forum, while application launches are reviewed via centralized expert risk reviews and application-focused forums.
For long-term and structural risks, our AGI Futures Council—consisting of senior management and Alphabet’s Board of Directors—provides perspectives and recommendations to our Board and management team on long-term opportunities, risks, and impacts associated with the development of AGI.
Frequency of Reviews and Trigger Events
Our risk management practices are fundamentally iterative.
Our approach evolves with developments in the underlying technology, new and emerging risks, and as new measurement techniques emerge, such as AI-assisted evaluations.
To assess whether a model contributes to identified safety risks, we conduct a critical capability assessment against Threshold/Critical Capability Levels (T/CCLs) prior to its initial external deployment. For subsequent model iterations, we execute material capability change assessments during post-training—evaluating specific checkpoints based on provenance, size, modality, and benchmark performance—to identify meaningful capability increases that could alter our risk determination. This monitoring relies on "early warning evaluations" and defined "alert thresholds"—mechanisms designed to flag when a Critical Capability Level (CCL) may be reached before a full critical capability assessment is repeated—which can be dynamically adjusted or run more frequently if the observed rate of progress diminishes our established safety buffers.
Our Frontier Safety Framework will be reviewed at least once a year—more frequently if we have reasonable grounds to believe the adequacy of the Framework or our adherence to it has been materially undermined. The process will involve (i) an assessment of the Framework’s appropriateness for the management of significant and severe risk, drawing on information sources such as record of adherence to the framework, relevant high-quality research, information shared through industry forums, and evaluation results, as necessary, and (ii) an assessment of our adherence to the Framework.
Distinctions Between Types of AI Systems
We proactively assess and tailor our risk management approach based on the specific type and capability of the AI system:
Frontier AI Models: Governed by the Frontier Safety Framework, which is built around capability thresholds called Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) intended to address severe risks like misuse and deceptive alignment.
Agentic AI & Personal Intelligence: In this agentic era—where AI systems autonomously interact with services and users—we require a new testing paradigm; our Novel AI Testing team was formed to spearhead evaluations at scale for new AI systems, such as advanced agents and Personal Intelligence.
Artificial General Intelligence (AGI): Managed with a focus on long-term, structural risks, exploring four main risk areas—misuse, misalignment, accidents, and structural risks—under the guidance of the AGI Futures Council and the approach detailed in Google Deepmind’s AGI Safety paper.

question: Please describe any measures used to ensure data quality and fairness across the data collection and curation stage (e.g., dataset audits, filtering training data to remove harmful content or personal information, fine-tuning on curated data, use of moderation tools, assessment of limitations to model generalisability).
answer:
We ensure data quality and fairness across the AI lifecycle through robust dataset audits, rigorous pre-training safety filtering, and supervised fine-tuning. We deploy a combination of automated and human-led moderation tools to steer outputs away from harm, and we actively document known limitations regarding generalisability to mitigate unfair bias.
Dataset Audits, as outlined in our AI Principles, we are committed to employing rigorous design, testing, monitoring, and safeguards to mitigate unintended or harmful outcomes and avoid unfair bias. 
To ensure this, governance requirements for models focus on filtering training data for quality, model performance, and adherence to policies, as well as documenting training techniques in technical reports and model cards. Furthermore, we also prioritize neutral and inclusive design principles, with a goal of minimizing unfair bias.
Filtering Training Data we apply safety filtering to our pre-training data for frontier models for our strictest policies. For a subset of our training data, we add control tags, e.g., based on classifier-annotated labels of the text’s toxicity. Additionally, as part of making pre-trained models safe and reliable, we used automated techniques to filter out certain personal information and other sensitive data from training sets.
Fine-Tuning on Curated Data Following initial data collection and filtering, we proactively mitigate risks through both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to ensure models are aligned with our content safety policies. For example, we used extensive fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback to align our instruction-tuned models with responsible behaviors.
Use of Moderation Tools To enforce our policies at scale, we use a combination of automated systems and human reviews to engage in continuous post-launch monitoring to improve our AI models and products, and detect activity and behavior that suggests misuse of our consumer products. Additionally, we deploy out-of-model mitigations, such as safety filters and conditional system instructions, to provide additional layers of protection by identifying, filtering out, or steering model output away from harmful or inappropriate content. We also leverage our Search tools to factually ground responses that require fresh or authoritative information.
Assessments of Limitations to Model Generalisability Training data, including from publicly available sources, reflects a diversity of perspectives and opinions. We continue to research how to use this data in a way that ensures that an LLM’s response incorporates a wide range of viewpoints, while minimizing inaccurate overgeneralizations and biases. To offer transparency, external model cards and technical reports are published regularly to provide essential information on models, including known limitations, mitigation approaches, and safety performance.

question: Please indicate, if relevant, the team or role responsible for overseeing secure testing and whether this responsibility is shared across multiple teams and/or functions.
answer:
Our governance process is grounded in a multi-layered oversight structure to govern secure testing throughout the AI system lifecycle. Responsibility is distributed across specialized central functions, creative red-teaming units, and senior governance councils:
Central Security and Reliability Teams: Our frontier models are developed, trained, tested, and stored within our own infrastructure, where we apply our Secure AI Framework (SAIF) throughout the AI lifecycle—supported by central security teams and a security, safety, and reliability organization consisting of engineers and researchers with world-class expertise.
Frontier Model Testing & External Partnerships: For model-level frontier testing, the Google DeepMind Responsibility Team operates directly within model development. Their core mission is to proactively track emerging risks, conduct structural safety evaluations (such as red-teaming), and align future models with ethical frameworks before deployment. Additionally, we work with external expert organizations through our External Safety Testing Program. These experts independently test and provide feedback on frontier safety domains. The team also actively collaborates with independent groups like the U.K. AI Security Institute and is a founding member of the Frontier Model Forum.
Application Testing: At the application/product level, our Content Adversarial Red Team (CART) proactively identifies unknown risks in our AI systems, enabling us to mitigate before launch. To evaluate our most advanced frontier systems, our Novel AI Testing team was formed to spearhead evaluations at scale for new AI systems, such as advanced agents and Personal Intelligence.
Security-focused red teaming: Our AI Red Team combines security and AI expertise to simulate attackers who might target AI systems; based on threat intelligence from teams like the Google Threat Intelligence Group, this unit explores how AI features can cause security issues, recommends improvements, and helps ensure that real-world attackers are detected and thwarted before they cause damage.
Governance Councils: Our model launches are reviewed at Google DeepMind’s Launch Review forum, which approves model releases, and our many application launches are reviewed systematically via launch infrastructure and centralized expert risk reviews, as well as via various application-focused launch review forums. These launch-specific forums are complemented by our Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) Futures Council, which consists of members of senior management and our Board of Directors.
Technical Description of Security Measures in Testing
Because we understand that AI, as a still-emerging transformative technology, involves evolving complexities and risks, we pursue AI responsibly by grounding our testing processes in the systematic application of technical controls to isolate risks and rigorously validate frontier models prior to deployment.
Testing Environments and Target Isolation Testing is performed in appropriately secured environments. Our frontier models are developed, trained, tested, and stored within our infrastructure, where we can apply our Secure AI Framework (SAIF) throughout the AI lifecycle, ensuring that any external trusted testing groups also receive secure access to test models. To address the safety and scalability challenges inherent in live internet testing of agentic products, where appropriate, we either restrict internet access during evals or require human-in-the-loop approval. This allows us to proactively identify and mitigate high harm risks without exposing the public web to potential harm. Additionally, we mandate that the processing of untrusted inputs occurs within sandboxed environments. A gradual approach to deployment serves as a critical risk mitigation—starting with testing internally, then releasing to trusted testers externally, before opening up to a small portion of our user base.
Containment, Capability Restrictions, and Controls To protect frontier models against adversarial inputs, we deploy robust cybersecurity controls and repeatable mitigations. For prompt injections and jailbreaks, we apply robust filtering and processing of inputs and outputs, while thorough training, tuning, and evaluation processes help fortify the model against these attacks. For data poisoning, we implement data sanitization, secure AI systems, enable access controls, and deploy mechanisms to ensure data and model integrity.
Agentic systems require a multi-layer defense strategy. We employ a hybrid defense-in-depth strategy that combines deterministic measures with dynamic, reasoning-based defenses to achieve a layered safety and security strategy. For example, in Chrome, we use a combination of rule-based and LLM-based approaches to limit agents permitted actions. This mechanism vets agents' actions against the user’s stated goal, rejecting misaligned steps. Ultimately, this comprehensive strategy combines human-in-the-loop expertise with AI-assisted scale to enable data-driven safety and security assessments.
Audit Logging, Monitoring, and Test-Data Curation We maintain oversight during evaluations by implementing automated monitoring agents that log interactions and assess the compliance of the agent being tested in real-time in certain contexts. Automatic testing for security vulnerabilities helps us assess code risks dynamically. To optimize test-data quality by design, we use automated techniques to filter out certain personal information and other sensitive data from training sets. Furthermore, we invest in "few shot" learning methodologies where an AI creates a synthetic testing set based on inputs from experts—significantly accelerating the testing scale when compared with the manual human creation of testing sets.

question: Describe key privacy measures and data-protection standards applied.
answer:
As outlined in our AI Principles, we are committed to promoting privacy and security. We employ a comprehensive approach to protect privacy and sensitive data across the AI lifecycle.
Data Governance and Lineage: We utilize technical controls and governance processes to ensure data is used safely and in compliance with policies. Protecting data requires both technical controls to enable safe data use at scale, and governance processes to ensure that companies have visibility and control over how their data is used. This fundamentally requires understanding data and ensuring it has sufficient metadata, controlling the data and implementing policies to allow or disallow usage based on attributes, transforming data to enable policy-compliant usage, and maintaining human oversight.
Encryption and Infrastructure Security: To prevent the disclosure of confidential or sensitive data, robust encryption standards are applied to user data both at rest and in transit. We start by building on our best-in-class security infrastructure and implement additional industry-leading safeguards to ensure that this data remains protected even as it powers new AI experiences. We’ve also done work to increase resistance to prompt injections and have improved protection against misuse via cyberattacks.
Privacy-Enhancing Technologies (PETs): Because privacy risks are highly context-dependent, our deployment decisions are guided by a risk-based framework rather than a single, one-size-fits-all approach. Furthermore, we remain committed to advancing research in the application of Privacy-Enhancing Technologies (PETs) to the AI lifecycle, such as applying differential privacy to LLMs in the context of trade-offs such as reduction in training stability, significantly increasing batch size, and computation costs. Our PETs research facilitated the release of VaultGemma–the largest (1B-parameters) open, DP-trained language model as of the date of release. This was a significant step forward in the journey toward building AI that is both powerful and private by design.
User Controls and Training Limitations: When deploying advanced AI systems, we build in strict user controls. Users have a choice on whether or not to connect new data sources to the Gemini App or Search AI Mode, and they can also choose to engage in conversations without personalization, and set their activity to auto-delete. If users opt in, we use our security infrastructure to securely connect data through Personal Intelligence, ensuring it is protected.

Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include model information (characteristics of the AI model relevant to the risk it may pose with its critical capabilities), evaluation results (such as details about the evaluation design, the results, and any robustness tests), and mitigation plans (descriptions of our mitigation plans and how they are expected to reduce the risk). question: If yes, describe how research or good practices are shared (e.g., publications, conferences, collaborations with other sectors).
answer:
We are committed to transparently sharing research and best practices to benefit the broader ecosystem. Because we understand that AI, as a still-emerging transformative technology, involves evolving complexities and risks, we work with stakeholders across the technology sector, government, and civil society regarding AI policies, remain abreast of emerging challenges, and establish, share, and learn from industry best practices and research.
 
Publications and Public Updates
We actively publish our findings, risk management methodologies, and research-backed guidelines across multiple public platforms to ensure accessible transparency:
Research Papers: We have continuously published research papers on responsible AI topics, many of which are relevant to addressing or managing risk. These are available to the public on Google Research’s publications repository and Google DeepMind’s publications archive. Our publications address specific, critical risk domains - including holistic safety evaluations, the study of misuses of generative AI, and broader ethical concerns regarding advanced AI systems.
Blogs and Reports: To reach audiences beyond the specialized research community, we share updates on dedicated platforms—such as research.google/blog, deepmind.google/blog/, publicpolicy.google and The Keyword blog, as well as in our annual Responsible AI Progress Report.
External and Contextual Frameworks: We contribute to external whitepapers in partnership with multi-stakeholder consortia—such as the Advertising Council Research Institute’s “Calibrating Trustworthiness in GenAI”. Additionally, we publish policy papers and frameworks for addressing and managing risk, such as "The TRUST Framework: A Policy Approach to Agentic AI," designed to provide guiding principles for the governance of AI agents
 
Tools and Actionable Resources
We make public many of our best practices for identifying, assessing, and evaluating risk via the Responsible AI Toolkit, which includes a methodology to build classifiers tailored to a specific policy with limited number of datapoints, as well as existing Google Cloud off-
the-shelf classifiers served via API. The toolkit also features tools such as ShieldGemma—a series of state-of-the-art safety classifiers that application developers can apply to detect and mitigate harmful content in AI model input and outputs—specifically targeting hate speech, harassment, sexually explicit content, and dangerous content.
 
Cross-Sector Partnerships and Collaborations
We heavily emphasize structured, cross-sector partnerships to develop technical standards, build joint solutions, and securely share threat intelligence:
Multi-Stakeholder Working Groups: We support the wider ecosystem with AI safety practices and standards by participating in working groups within global organizations—including MLCommons, the World Economic Forum’s (WEF) AI Governance Alliance, the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA), Thorn, Partnership on AI (PAI), the Frontier Model Forum (FMF), and government partners, such as the U.K. AI Security Institute. As of June, we are also founding members of the Appia Foundation – an international group that builds on standards from bodies like ISO/IEC to create clear criteria, allowing organizations across the AI value chain to prove they meet their obligations, including those related to managing AI risk.  
Information Sharing Agreements: To stay ahead of emerging vulnerabilities, we signed a first-of-its-kind agreement with fellow members of the FMF—designed to facilitate information-sharing about threats, vulnerabilities, and capability advances unique to frontier AI.
Joint Governance Initiatives: We launched the Coalition for Secure AI (CoSAI) with industry partners to share security expertise under the guidance of OASIS Open. Additionally, we have collaborated with PAI to jointly launch responsibility frameworks for safe deployment, synthetic media, and data enrichment sourcing.
 
Ecosystem Funding and Community Engagement
To foster independent validation and incentivize the global research community to proactively uncover potential system limitations, we invest in external safety initiatives:
Data-Centric Challenges: We partnered with universities across India, Nigeria, Ghana, to conduct community-centered harms analysis of image generation models. Our methodology and findings are shared publicly for advancing global AI safety standards. We continue to closely partner with MLCommons and Korea AI Safety Institute, among others to build culturally-specific and geographically-relevant AI safety datasets.
Multi-agent AI Safety Research: In a partnership between Google DeepMind, Google.org, Schmidt Sciences, the Cooperative AI Foundation, the Advanced Research and Invention Agency,we launched a new $10M technical research fund to help understand how multi-agent systems behave, how to mitigate new potential risks, and how these independent systems interact safely and predictably across various networks.

User Disclosure, Documentation, and FAQs Our governance process is grounded in setting clear, consistent expectations for end-users across the digital ecosystem.
Mechanisms we employ in this space include interstitials and FAQs, such as the FAQ for Gemini Apps, that provide users with the knowledge and answers that they are engaging with an advanced system.
Where appropriate, our generative-AI products use disclaimers to set clear expectations — such as reminding people that the AI-generated outputs may contain inaccuracies and that they should take steps to verify information generated by the tool.
We proactively empower users with robust knowledge about Personal Intelligence — from acknowledging its limitations to providing users with resources such as the Gemini app Help Center and the AI Mode Help Center to learn more about how the system interacts with their data.
Persistent Indicators, Labeling, and Provenance Information Because we understand that AI involves evolving complexities, we implement by design specific technical mitigations to verify authenticity and surface provenance signals.
We developed SynthID to help address issues around provenance by embedding digital watermarks directly into AI-generated content — including text, audio, images, and video.
In 2025, we announced SynthID Detector, a verification portal that allows users to quickly and efficiently upload content and scan for SynthID watermarks, and identify if content was generated or modified by Google’s AI tools.
Furthermore, we continue to integrate these standards directly into our hardware and services — such as Pixel 10, which is the first phone to implement content credentials within its native camera app, and the inclusion of C2PA metadata into images generated by our generative AI image model, Nano Banana Pro.
In May 2026, we added C2PA content credential detection to the Gemini App to share more signals with users about the origin and authenticity of online content. We also announced that we were expanding C2PA and SynthID to Search and Chrome so even more people can get helpful context relevant to the origin and authenticity of a given piece of content.
These technical solutions are complemented by Backstory — an experimental AI tool that helps identify whether an image was AI-generated, even without watermarks, or whether it is authentic but presented in a misleading context, investigating how it has been used on the internet and providing other helpful metadata.

Implementation and Technical Mechanisms Because we understand that AI, as a still-emerging transformative technology, involves evolving complexities and risks, we pursue AI responsibly by implementing a multi-faceted approach to provenance using both invisible watermarking and manifest disclosures. Our technical implementation operates sequentially across different media types:
Latent Disclosure via SynthID: We developed SynthID to help address issues around provenance by embedding digital watermarks directly into AI-generated content — including text, audio, images, and video. These watermarks are imperceptible to humans but remain detectable by specialized software. We have improved SynthID to identify text and video generated by the Gemini app and web experience.
Detection Tools: To enable verification, we announced SynthID Detector — a verification portal that allows users to quickly and efficiently upload content and scan for SynthID watermarks to identify if content was generated or modified by our AI tools. Furthermore, to help more organizations identify AI-generated media, we are launching a new AI Content Detection API on Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. In May 2026, we added C2PA content credential detection to the Gemini App to share more signals with users about the origin and authenticity of online content. We also announced that we were expanding C2PA and SynthID to Search and Chrome so even more people can get helpful context relevant to the origin and authenticity of a given piece of content. 
Manifest Disclosure and Context: We deploy visible notices to ensure audience awareness. For example, YouTube requires creators to disclose when they have created realistic altered or synthetic content, displaying a visible label to indicate when the content being watched is synthetic.
International Technical Standards and Robustness We are actively working with industry partners to develop and implement the Content Credentials standard developed by the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA). We provided substantial contributions to the latest version (2.1) of the C2PA standard to ensure it meets the complex needs of modern hardware and software. Furthermore, we continue to integrate these standards directly into our hardware and services, such as Pixel 10, which is the first phone to implement content credentials within its native camera app, and the inclusion of C2PA metadata into images generated by our generative AI image model, Nano Banana Pro.
Collaborations and Investments We actively participate in, collaborate on, and invest in projects advancing AI safety, security, and trustworthiness. To advance the state of content authentication, we pursue multiple cross-cutting initiatives:
We joined the C2PA as a steering committee member to support this cross-industry effort to provide more transparency and context on digital content.
We joined the Partnership on AI (PAI) Synthetic Media Framework to jointly develop responsibility frameworks alongside industry peers.
We are executing joint R&D projects — partnering with NVIDIA to watermark AI-generated video from their Cosmos world foundation models. We have expanded this partnership on SynthID to other industry leaders such as OpenAI, Kakao and ElevenLabs.
We support open-source initiatives by making our in-house SynthID text watermarking tool available on Hugging Face — making it easier for any developer to apply watermarking for their generative text models and detect outputs from their own large language models.

Artefact manages AI risk across the full project lifecycle through its Data Science Project Checklist, which structures every AI project around six stages: problem framing and business justification (Plan and design), data access and quality assessment (Collect and process data), baseline definition and model development (Build, integrate and interpret model), performance, bias and reproducibility checks (Verify and validate), production-readiness review including external expert review and regulatory compliance (Deploy), and ongoing metric tracking, drift detection and rollback capability (Operate and monitor).

Reviews are triggered by project milestones (go-live decisions), by incidents, and by material changes to a deployed system; cross-cutting escalation is coordinated through our “AI Security Office”. In addition to the Standards of conduct for each of the “Planning,” “Social Implementation,” and “Maintenance and Management” phases, the Guiding Principles set forth the following seven Items to be addressed: “Safety,” “Privacy,” “Fairness, Equality, and Prevention of discrimination,” “Proper and responsible development and use,” “Transparency, Explainability and Accountability,” “Security,” and “Compliance.”
From these perspectives, we assess the purpose and context of AI use and treat as high risk any AI use that may have a significant impact on human life, fundamental human rights, individual dignity, or individuals’ autonomous decision-making. Where a risk is determined to be high, we consider and implement necessary risk mitigation measures and determine whether the AI may be used, taking into account the results of those measures.

question: How does your organization define and/or classify different types of risks related to AI?¹
answer:

Define enhanced safety measures for specific dangerous capability thresholds, that, once reached, require safeguards (e.g. capability threshold for dangerous Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear (CBRN), cybersecurity attacks, dangerous advanced autonomy capabilities, or other capabilities).
Align with specific external frameworks, standards, reports, and/or guidance documents such as taxonomies, classification systems, and/or sets of definitions for risk areas (e.g. the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the ISO/IEC 42001, the OECD AI Principles, the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, the International AI Safety Report). (please specify): MGOIT aligns its AI risk management practices with the following external frameworks: (1) ISO/IEC 27001:2022 — the organisation is certified, and its information security management system (risk assessment, data encryption, access control, incident management) forms the operational foundation for AI-related risk controls; (2) the OECD AI Principles and the Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organisations Developing Advanced AI Systems — MGOIT reported under the HAIP Reporting Framework 1.0 (published in the OECD 2025 report 'How are AI developers managing risks?') and uses the Code of Conduct's action areas as a structuring reference for its internal AI governance practices; (3) the EU AI Act risk-based classification system, used to assess and categorise client-facing AI applications during scoping and design.

As an application developer and deployer, MGOIT does not train frontier models and therefore does not operate formal capability-based risk thresholds. Instead, we apply decision criteria and governance processes at the project and system level to determine when an AI risk would be unreasonable:
(1) Use-case gating at scoping. Before development begins, each AI feature is assessed against the EU AI Act risk classification and our internal criteria. We consider risk unreasonable — and decline or redesign the use case — when an AI system would make fully automated decisions with significant impact on individuals (e.g. financial, employment, or safety-relevant outcomes) without meaningful human review, or when the client's data governance cannot support the required level of data protection.
(2) Human-in-the-loop as a graduated mitigation. Mitigations scale with impact: low-stakes outputs (e.g. document drafting, information retrieval) ship with user-facing review; higher-impact outputs (e.g. financial calculations, offers, compliance-relevant content) require explicit human approval before any downstream effect. Edge cases detected in testing are routed to mandatory human review paths.
(3) Pre-deployment testing in secure environments. AI features are tested in isolated environments with anonymised or synthetic data before production exposure, including adversarial and edge-case testing for bias and incorrect outputs.
(4) Agentic AI specifics. Where we build agentic capabilities (multi-step workflows, tool use, integrations), agents operate under scoped permissions: restricted tool access, no autonomous write-access to production systems of record without an approval gate, full action logging for auditability, and rollback paths. Autonomy level is treated as a risk dimension in itself — broader autonomy requires stricter approval gates and monitoring.
(5) Escalation and stop criteria. If testing or production monitoring reveals behaviour that cannot be mitigated to an acceptable level (persistent hallucination in a high-impact path, unmitigable bias, data leakage risk), the feature is withheld or rolled back until redesigned. This decision sits with the technical leadership (CTO and technical leads), not with delivery deadlines.

MGOIT's AI risk management runs through the full project lifecycle on a single governance chain: (1) scoping — use-case risk assessment (EU AI Act classification, internal criteria) with authority to decline or redesign unreasonable use cases; (2) design — graduated human-in-the-loop mechanisms and, for agentic systems, scoped permissions, approval gates on write actions, and full action logging; (3) pre-deployment — testing in secure staging environments with anonymised/synthetic data, edge-case and bias checks, security and GDPR review under our ISO/IEC 27001:2022 ISMS; (4) deployment — technical lead and CTO sign-off plus client UAT acceptance, phased release and rollback paths; (5) operations — monitoring, incident management with committed SLAs, and corrective actions feeding back into risk criteria and testing checklists.

Jus Mundi does not currently rely on a single quantitative threshold to determine when an AI-related risk becomes “unreasonable.” Instead, severe AI risks are assessed through a risk-based governance process aligned with the organization’s role as a legal intelligence and technology provider, and with its broader security, privacy, compliance and AI governance frameworks. The most relevant references are ISO/IEC 42001, ISO 27001, the EU AI Act, OECD AI Principles, data protection requirements, and internal information security and risk management policies.
A risk may be considered unreasonable or intolerable when, after considering available mitigations, it could create a severe impact on individuals, clients, the legal process, confidentiality, security, regulatory compliance, or the integrity of Jus Mundi’s services. Examples include: unauthorized disclosure or processing of confidential legal or personal data; AI outputs that could materially mislead users in legal research or decision-making if presented without appropriate caveats or human review; system behavior that could compromise the availability, integrity or security of the platform; discriminatory or unfair outputs in sensitive contexts; or autonomous actions performed without adequate authorization, traceability or human oversight.
In practice, Jus Mundi evaluates these risks using decision criteria such as severity of potential harm, likelihood, scale of exposure, sensitivity of the data involved, reversibility of harm, detectability, regulatory impact, customer impact, and the effectiveness of controls. Risks that remain high or critical after mitigation require escalation to the relevant governance bodies and accountable functions, including Security, Legal/DPO, Product, Engineering and AI governance stakeholders. Deployment may be blocked, delayed, limited to a controlled environment, or subject to additional safeguards where residual risk is not acceptable.
Mitigations are graduated according to the capability and risk profile of the AI system. Lower-risk use cases may require standard controls such as documentation, user guidance, access control, logging, human review and monitoring. Higher-risk use cases may require enhanced review, security and privacy assessments, vendor due diligence, model or application testing, stricter access restrictions, output validation, contractual safeguards, phased deployment, incident response procedures and formal approval before release.
For generative AI, Jus Mundi pays particular attention to hallucination, explainability, source attribution, confidentiality, prompt/input handling, copyright and data protection risks, and user reliance on AI-generated outputs. For agentic AI or tool-using systems, additional scrutiny is applied to autonomy, permissions, ability to take actions, access to sensitive systems or data, auditability, rollback capacity, and human-in-the-loop controls. Agentic capabilities would be restricted or prohibited where they could perform high-impact actions without appropriate authorization, monitoring, and intervention mechanisms.

question: Please briefly describe your organization’s decision-making process for deploying an AI model or system including: who has decision authority; what evidence and criteria are required (e.g., performance, safety/security, robustness, fairness, privacy, compliance, independent external testing, evaluation, validation and verification (TEVV) or assurance); contextual caveats or limitations required in interpreting risk evaluation metric results; what approvals/sign-offs are needed; and what safeguards (e.g., mitigations, monitoring, or phased release) must be in place to move into deployment.
answer:
Jus Mundi uses a risk-based approval process before deploying AI systems. Decision authority depends on the risk level and involves the Product and Engineering owners, with Security, Legal/DPO, and AI governance review where confidentiality, privacy, compliance, customer impact, or service integrity may be affected.
Before release, the team reviews the intended use, data involved, vendor or model assessment, security and privacy risks, testing results, output quality, robustness, misuse scenarios, access controls, monitoring, and compliance requirements. Deployment is allowed only when performance is acceptable for the intended use, critical risks are mitigated, and the residual risk is within the organization’s risk appetite.
Higher-risk or customer-facing systems require additional sign-off and may be escalated to governance bodies. Required safeguards may include human oversight, access controls, data minimization, logging, user guidance, source attribution, monitoring, incident response, rollback mechanisms, and phased deployment. For agentic AI, Jus Mundi applies stricter controls on autonomy, permissions, approval gates, audit trails, and the ability to suspend unsafe behavior.

These inputs are assessed for severity, likelihood, affected systems or users, data sensitivity, regulatory impact, and relevance to Jus Mundi’s AI use cases. When an incident or external report indicates a new or increased risk, the relevant AI system risk assessment is updated and the issue is escalated to the appropriate Product, Engineering, Security, Legal/DPO, or AI governance stakeholders. Corrective actions may include fixing vulnerabilities, changing prompts or model behavior, improving monitoring, strengthening access controls, adding user guidance or human review, restricting or pausing a feature, notifying affected parties where required, and updating policies, procedures, or controls. Lessons learned are incorporated into future testing, deployment criteria, incident response, and AI governance reviews.

question: How does your organization define and/or classify different types of risks related to AI?¹
answer:
Maintain an internal taxonomy, classification system, and/or set of risk area definitions
Align with specific external frameworks, standards, reports, and/or guidance documents such as taxonomies, classification systems, and/or sets of definitions for risk areas (e.g. the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the ISO/IEC 42001, the OECD AI Principles, the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, the International AI Safety Report). (please specify): METI/MIC AI Guidelines for Business (Ver. 1.1) and its Appendix; Hiroshima AI Process (HAIP) International Code of Conduct; OECD AI Principles; NIST AI Risk Management Framework; Japan AI Safety Institute (AISI) Guide to Evaluation Perspectives on AI Safety, and its healthcare edition, the Guide to Evaluation Perspectives on AI Safety in the Healthcare Sector (published April 2026), which Ubie co-developed as leader of the AISI Healthcare Sub-Working Group on behalf of The Japan Digital Health Alliance (JaDHA); JaDHA Guide to the Utilization of Generative AI for Healthcare Providers; the Two Guidelines from Three Ministries (the MHLW Guidelines for the Safety Management of Medical Information Systems and the METI/MIC Safety Management Guidelines for Information System and Service Providers Handling Medical Information); ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (certified). Alignment with ISO/IEC 42001 is under consideration.
Consult with external stakeholders (e.g., from academia, industry groups, civil society, or standard development organisations) when developing or updating risk taxonomies

Ubie does not use numeric capability thresholds, as we are not a foundation model developer. We apply decision criteria and governance processes instead.
Decision criteria. Severity is determined on two axes: imminence and severity of harm. Inputs are the use case, the users, the sensitivity of the data, the influence of outputs on clinical or health decisions, the degree of AI autonomy, whether human confirmation is in place, and whether an external foundation model is used. Because health and medical information can influence user behaviour, we treat three points as non-negotiable: our services provide general information; they do not constitute diagnosis or treatment; and they complement rather than replace human judgment.
How mitigations are graduated. Mitigations escalate with the assessed level of risk: (1) baseline - prompt and guardrail design, input and output filtering, disclaimers, terms of use; (2) elevated - mandatory medical review by physicians before release, sample evaluation of generative outputs, adversarial testing, and restriction of the intended purpose; (3) high - limitation of the scope of provision, access rights restricted so that highly confidential data is accessible only to the medical institution concerned, mandatory human confirmation with the original source always retrievable, and additional operational procedures and customer training; (4) unacceptable - postponement or non-release, or suspension of a feature already in service.
Generative AI and agentic AI. For generative AI features we assume that outputs of external foundation models may contain bias or hallucination, and we design for verification rather than trust: the original text is displayed by default with the AI-generated summary shown alongside (our "safety net structure"), sources are cited, and inputs and creation history are logged for ex post verification. Agentic AI systems that plan or act to a partial extent are under evaluation. Because an error in the medical domain can be irreversible, our governance for agentic capabilities requires an explicit boundary of autonomous action, a human decision point before any action affecting a patient or a medical record, transparency of the decision logic, and evaluation against the AISI Guide to Evaluation Perspectives on AI Safety in the Healthcare Sector before any phased introduction. Evaluation perspectives for agentic AI are being organised through our research organization Ubie Lab and the AISI Healthcare Sub-Working Group.
Governance. Risk assessment is performed by dedicated specialists independent of the development and business units in order to ensure objectivity. A two-layer structure - the Generative AI Promotion Team on the promotion side and the Risk and Compliance Committee (legal, security, public relations and other functions) on the risk side - shares information and deliberates trade-offs, and the Trust & Safety Team performs cross-product quality management. This structure is featured as an advanced case (Column 11) in the Appendix to the METI/MIC AI Guidelines for Business (Ver. 1.1).

question: Please briefly describe your organization’s decision-making process for deploying an AI model or system including: who has decision authority; what evidence and criteria are required (e.g., performance, safety/security, robustness, fairness, privacy, compliance, independent external testing, evaluation, validation and verification (TEVV) or assurance); contextual caveats or limitations required in interpreting risk evaluation metric results; what approvals/sign-offs are needed; and what safeguards (e.g., mitigations, monitoring, or phased release) must be in place to move into deployment.
answer: Decision authority. Release of an AI feature is decided by the responsible product team on the basis of a cross-product review by the Trust & Safety Team. Risk assessment is performed by dedicated specialists independent of the development and business units in order to ensure objectivity. Where a material concern remains, the decision escalates to the Risk and Compliance Committee (legal, security, public relations and other functions), which deliberates the trade-off between AI utilization and risk together with the Generative AI Promotion Team. This two-layer structure is featured as an advanced case (Column 11) in the Appendix to the METI/MIC AI Guidelines for Business (Ver. 1.1). Evidence and criteria required. Review and approval gates are applied at each stage. At the planning stage we assess the use case, the users, data sensitivity, and impacts on medical safety, privacy and security. Before release, the evidence required against defined test criteria comprises: functional testing; medical review by physicians of clinical accuracy; sample evaluation of generative AI outputs, including hallucination and source attribution; security assessment, including prompt injection; privacy review covering the scope of data sent to external foundation models and retention in logs; legal and regulatory compliance review (Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Act, Medical Practitioners Act, Act on the Protection of Personal Information, and the Two Guidelines from Three Ministries); and fairness review across disease, age, sex, expression of symptoms, and region or access to healthcare. Independent external assurance is used for information security, through ISMS (ISO/IEC 27001:2022) audit and security assessment. Contextual caveats in interpreting risk evaluation metric results. Evaluation results are read as conditional rather than absolute. Sample evaluation of generative outputs is not exhaustive, so a passing result is not evidence of the absence of hallucination. Benchmark and test-set performance does not transfer directly to real clinical language, which includes dialects, abbreviations and non-standard medical terminology. Because our products are built on external foundation models, results are valid only for the model and version tested, and are re-examined when the model, version or data integration method changes. For these reasons we do not treat any single metric as a sole release criterion, and human confirmation is retained as the controlling safeguard. Approvals and sign-offs. Confirmation of conformity with our quality standards by the Trust & Safety Team is required before release. Deployment at a medical institution additionally requires confirmation of that customer's security and operational requirements under contract. A fresh security review is triggered by material changes to external foundation models, cloud services or data integration methods, and by amendments to applicable laws or guidelines. Safeguards required to move into deployment. Prompt and guardrail design with input and output filtering; a human confirmation step for any output that materially affects a care decision; the "safety net structure", in which the original text is displayed by default and can always be referenced; access rights restricted so that highly confidential data of a medical institution is accessible only to that institution; cautionary notices in wording and UI; operating procedures and customer training; and continuous log and error monitoring after release. Where risk warrants it, we limit the scope of provision or release in phases. Where material risk remains, we postpone or do not release.

question: Following deployment, how do you use incident reports — including those shared by other organizations — to identify emerging issues, update risk assessments, and trigger corrective actions.
answer:
Yes. Internally, incidents that occur or are reported, inquiries, and feedback from medical institutions are managed centrally in an incident management tool. For each we record the type, scope of impact, root cause, detection channel and recurrence-prevention measures, and we then check whether the same type of risk exists in other products or other use cases. Root cause analysis and recurrence-prevention measures are documented as post-mortems.
Externally, we continuously refer to the checklists and case examples in the AISI Guide to Evaluation Perspectives on AI Safety in the Healthcare Sector and the JaDHA Guide to the Utilization of Generative AI for Healthcare Providers, to publicly available information on medical information systems, personal data protection and cybersecurity, and to incident cases reported by other companies and other industries - including cases outside healthcare where the failure mode is transferable.
Updating risk assessments. Findings feed back into our internal risk taxonomy and its categories, into the test criteria applied before release (new test items are added), and into internal education. Corrective actions triggered include revision of prompts, guardrails, UI and explanatory text; additional output filters; updates to our medical information database; security patches; review of permission settings; restriction or suspension of a feature; and revision of operational guides, templates and customer training. Where notification is required by law or contract, we notify affected customer medical institutions and users, and report to public authorities such as the Personal Information Protection Commission. Knowledge is shared with the industry through the AISI Healthcare Sub-Working Group, JaDHA, and the AI Governance Association (AIGA).
